#108514. Bypassing iOS Safari's 60 FPS Limit to Build Web Applications That Feel Native

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2172 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rida ↗ Open Full Page

Bypassing iOS Safari's 60 FPS Limit to Build Web Applications That Feel Native

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2172 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rida

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Devon Govett of React Aria posted “Scrolling is All You Need: Building a Swipeable Sheet” back in October, and in it he talked about his team developing a sheet component that cleverly leverages the physics and smooth interactions provided by native browsers to provide the illusion of a native interaction.
  • More recently, Jordan Walke, creator of React, posted a video of an experiment on X showing a convincing native-like mobile interaction using DOM & CSS.
  • What the video Jordan Walke posted doesn’t show is that, unless you flip the “Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps” flag buried deep within the Safari developer settings on iOS, WebKit limits requestAnimationFrame to just 60 Hz on a 120 Hz screen, and on a regular page, touch and pointer events are held to that same rate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rida F'kih · November 20, 2026 · 10 min read.

Devon Govett of React Aria posted “Scrolling is All You Need: Building a Swipeable Sheet” back in October, and in it he talked about his team developing a sheet component that cleverly leverages the physics and smooth interactions provided by native browsers to provide the illusion of a native interaction.

More recently, Jordan Walke, creator of React, posted a video of an experiment on X showing a convincing native-like mobile interaction using DOM & CSS. It re-established a long-lived itch that I’ve had, and prompted this response from me. It’s something I could never justify building, however. Anything I built using this method would be pegged to 60 FPS.

What the video Jordan Walke posted doesn’t show is that, unless you flip the “Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps” flag buried deep within the Safari developer settings on iOS, WebKit limits requestAnimationFrame to just 60 Hz on a 120 Hz screen, and on a regular page, touch and pointer events are held to that same rate. This is what makes even the best mobile websites feel irritating to use.

Recent findings suggest that how can I make this experience suck less without resorting to flags? Let’s call back to the React Aria piece. The reason it feels so nice is that scrolling is the responsibility of the compositor. It runs in its own thread. It moves, clips and fades without a JavaScript round-trip.

Recent findings suggest that finger to digitizer, digitizer to compositor, compositor to GPU. This will become the basis of our interaction.

Industry observers note that behold, two grids. They both move a square when you drag. The one on the left uses JavaScript events and sets the transform attribute in CSS, while the one on the right simply places a square in a scrollable area.

If you’re on iOS Safari, you’ll immediately be able to tell which is which because one refreshes at most 60 times a second in a renderer pass, while the other uses the compositor.

Recent findings suggest that in order to leverage the power of the scroll area, we need to find a way to read the scroll position outside of the renderer. If we can do that, we can treat it like a trackpad, or use it to “extract” native bounce, physics, momentum, etc., and apply them directly from the compositor to our animations.

The point is, it’d be crazy flexible if we could just find a way to pull the values out of it frequently enough.

I measured scroll events updating 5 to 26 times per second during momentum scroll on an iPhone Duo. The best-case scenario is during slow, deliberate scrolls where it reaches almost 60 updates a second. Useless.

Instead, we’ll be aiming to read scrollTop and scrollLeft synchronously.

It has been revealed that first, I tried having a MessageChannel call itself recursively, which worked: but it produced 50,000 reads a second with just 80 distinct values. That’s a lot of waste and heat since it pins a CPU core.

According to recent reports, next failure was trying to use Atomics to wake at the screen’s refresh rate, which worked and similarly extracted 80 distinct positions every second, but the drawbacks were too great. Since it needs a SharedArrayBuffer, we’re forced to use COOP/COEP headers which break cross-origin assets on our website.

What finally worked was using a MessageChannel like before, throttling the next measurement to the next tick using a setTimeout according to the refresh rate of the device, phase-locked to vsync using requestAnimationFrame timestamps. I was nervous about this approach, but as you’ll see later, it panned out well. The only remaining drawback specific to this solution was easy to work around. iOS rounds performance.now() to the millisecond, so I derived the minimum time between draws from the refresh interval.

Each solution got us 80 position reads per second. Two-thirds towards our goal of 120 Hz input.

According to recent reports, safari’s UI process sends the web process one scroll position at a time, and waits for an acknowledgement from the web process before sending another. Anything that arrives in the meantime is overwritten. This was costing us dropped positions. Digging through WebKit yielded what we needed to get around this. It turns out that on every tick where the page has a rendering update queued, Safari flushes the position without waiting. An empty requestAnimationFrame loop is all we need to do that.

This bought us ~12.5% more reads, and brought us to 90 unique position reads per second.

I sort of assumed I had hit the limit of the aforementioned IPC, but it turns out that ProMotion was just deciding that there’s no need to render at a refresh rate higher than 90 Hz.

Industry observers note that squeezing out the last 30 Hz was trickier. A GPU-accelerated CSS animation lets the screen go to 120 Hz, but only while something is scrolling. So a tiny invisible scroller smooth-scrolls in the background, ready to boost us to the full ProMotion refresh rate whenever we need it.

Of course, we don’t want the display pegging to 120 Hz the entire time, so we reserve all the tricks we used to get there for times we expect animations to occur: touch events, scroll-derived animations, etc.

If the interaction you’re building doesn’t need momentum, rubber banding, or snapping, you can forego them entirely and just use a passive touchmove listener on the controller which fires at the full 120 Hz.

Recent findings suggest that just like that, we’re receiving updates from the controller at a full 120 Hz! Drag the grid below to see.

One glitch remains. scrollTop and scrollLeft are rounded to the nearest integer even though iOS scrolls with sub-point precision. Easy fix, thankfully. We just scale the scrollable surface up by the device pixel ratio, then its container back down by its reciprocal.

If you want to use the viewport itself as a controller, you can choose to invasively set the initial-scale in the same way, but this comes with some caveats. You’ll have to scale units by the DPR, disable text autosizing, and manually scale safe areas. You’ll also get tiny text-selection indicators. All trade-offs, but by no means required.

In a recent development, from here on out, I’ll refer to these scrolling grids as “controllers”, because they act exactly like one. All we have to do is make one invisible and lay it over where we want to read high-frequency input.

Note that the page itself can also be a controller, but Safari will throttle reported scroll positions to 10 Hz during the URL bar resize that happens when you change scroll direction. WebKit skips this if we give the page a scroll-driven animation that animates a non-GPU-accelerated attribute. I went with transitioning between two transparent colours for this page.

Now we get high-frequency input, but the DOM still only updates 60 times a second, so if we tried to leverage it as it stands, we’d just be updating a value twice for every frame that’s drawn. The user would get no benefit.

In a recent development, the vast majority of dragging interactions are already covered by our controllers, and predefined animations are covered by CSS animations. But what about more complicated interactions? What about computation-derived layouts? What about shaders?

Ask your search engine or AI of choice today “How to render canvas content on iOS at 120 Hz without feature flag?” and it will respond that this is a fundamental impossibility in iOS Safari. Even WebKit’s own bug tracker is full of people asking for it. Ink & Switch, game-engine makers. People even cite Capacitor & Tauri as resorting to private APIs.

Asking Google yields the following preamble.

There is no public web API or standard JavaScript workaround to force HTML5 (requestAnimationFrame) to run at 120 Hz on iOS Safari without changing the system feature flag.

Fable 5.2 shares the same sentiment.

Short answer: you can't, for JavaScript-drawn canvas frames. On iOS, WebKit caps page rendering updates (which is when canvas content is presented) at 60 Hz unless the user turns off the flag. No web API overrides it. […] Timer-based loops (setTimeout, MessageChannel) won't help, in my understanding: you can draw more often, but the result is still presented at the 60 Hz rendering patch. Low Power Mode throttles further.

Industry observers note that at first, I tunnel-visioned on scroll. I tried breaking workers, pre-rendering permutation “flip-books,” and even live-generating video. It was all too laggy, jagged, or required so much RAM the WebKit process just crashed.

Seven attempts later, and a whole lot of agents digging through WebKit’s source, I landed on this.

In WebKit on iOS, if we create a canvas element and call transferControlToOffscreen, we get an OffscreenCanvas back. The original canvas element becomes a placeholder, and WebKit (following the HTML specification’s recommendation) skips waiting for the next rendering pass when an OffscreenCanvas pushes a frame.

Unlike earlier attempts, without workarounds this is easy on the battery and only uses as much memory as is needed to support a higher-frequency backing store.

Recent findings suggest that jackpot. We now have 120 FPS rendering on iOS WebKit canvases.

Now we can take any input at 120 Hz, and render an output at that very same frame rate. The first thing I created for this was a small UI clone of Ando’s mobile application fitted with a Liquid Glass tab bar, buttons, and buttery smooth navigation interactions. Once installed as a PWA, I kept having to double-take to check I wasn’t in the native application.

Industry observers note that this page is fitted with two custom “Liquid Glass” elements in the viewport. Each of them renders at the full device refresh rate. We have to be very deliberate in order to do this in a way that is performant and convincing.

In a recent development, when the page first loads, we take a snapshot and load it into a WebGL texture. This texture is used as the foundation for a composite that is then fed into our shader.

As the page scrolls, we then sample the region beneath each component, which is all we need to produce our effect. Building it this way means that no matter how the content below it is built, it can decide the best way to keep the texture live.

Recent findings suggest that on this page, components using requestAnimationFrame for illustrative reasons enhancement the texture from the main thread. Components using OffscreenCanvas post their frames directly from their workers to the worker managing the texture. This keeps us off the main thread and lets us get shaders refreshing at 120 Hz.

After all that, the glass just samples a small region around where it would land on the composite texture and computes the frame.

Let’s build our Liquid Glass tab bar. We’ll start out by just drawing the underlying structure.

We’ll break this down into one controller for each button. Each controller sends us timestamped events: which controller is being used, and how much it has been dragged. We keep a short history of those samples, so we know when a press has moved far enough to count as a drag, and how fast the finger is moving. Nothing else. Everything else is derived from that.

We now build a state machine around this. Every frame, the newly introduced events go in, and a frame comes out: where the lens is, how far it has lifted and stretched, and how visible the pill is.

Finally, we apply some shaders to get a convincing Liquid Glass effect.

I built a benchmark environment and recorded an iPhone 18 Pro at 240 FPS, slowing it down to an eighth to benchmark the difference. The two oscillating squares measure inputs and renders.

Recent findings suggest that over three seconds of dragging, the controller version averaged 118 FPS while the pointer events version held a steady 60. Even in Low Power Mode, which traditionally limits you to 30, this approach gets you 60.

Industry observers note that liquid Glass was the target as an overblown example, but this unlocks a lot. For the first time, you can take input and render output at true device-native speeds on iOS Safari. Micro-interactions feel native and delightful, PWAs which ignored the aforementioned feature flag finally have a way to render at 120 Hz, and look at all the fun we had along the way!

Would I rebuild my entire application around this? No. Fact remains it’s completely within Apple’s rights and would not violate the HTML specification if they just decided to make OffscreenCanvas’ placeholder wait for the main thread rendering pass. They even have a strong track record of “party pooping” as was done shortly after Lochie Axon unveiled the web-haptics library. I’d much prefer they make these findings moot by disabling the feature flag and natively supporting ProMotion for websites, but Apple is Apple for a reason after all.

#108513. iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (876 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (876 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, gymKit has been one of Apple Watch’s smartest fitness features since it launched in 2017.
  • With iOS 27, Apple is expanding that idea beyond Apple Watch.
  • Sources indicate that the setup is simple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gymKit has been one of Apple Watch’s smartest fitness features since it launched in 2017. Tap your watch to compatible gym equipment, and Apple Watch shares your heart rate while the machine sends back metrics like distance, incline, pace, and calories.

With iOS 27, Apple is expanding that idea beyond Apple Watch. I tested the upcoming GymKit on iPhone and AirPods Pro 3 ($149, reg. $249) experience with a GymKit-compatible treadmill. It basically gives you the Apple Watch GymKit workout tracking experience, just without the watch. This could be useful in a lot of scenarios.

Sources indicate that the setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

It has been revealed that as a side note: Apple Watch has more accurate treadmill workout tracking as part of watchOS 27. GymKit remains the gold standard for accurate data, though.

In a recent development, gymKit also avoids two awkward gym habits. You don’t need to hold the treadmill’s metal heart-rate contacts while jogging. You also do not need to wear a Bluetooth heart-rate strap.

Sources indicate that airPods Pro 3 become the heart-rate source (and likely your podcast or music audio source as well). iPhone becomes the workout computer, which you can monitor during your workout. And the treadmill fills in the machine data while providing the surface for walking or running.

Apple has been moving more fitness features onto iPhone for years. iOS first made the Fitness app useful without Apple Watch as Apple Fitness+ leaned into iPhone as an entry point. AirPods Pro 3 pushed that further as the first AirPods with heart-rate tracking, after Apple tested the idea with Powerbeats Pro 2.

Sources indicate that iOS 27 brings those pieces together. GymKit on iPhone shouldn’t replace Apple Watch for people who wear one every day. Instead, it’s a great backup when your Apple Watch is dead, charging, or left at home.

It also gives iPhone and AirPods owners a taste of the Apple Watch experience, which could attract future Apple Watch customers.

Recent findings suggest that in testing with iOS 27 beta 1, my Exercise ring didn’t upgrade as I worked out without wearing Apple Watch. But after I put my watch back on, the Exercise ring caught up, and the workout appeared in Fitness with the right data.

My sample 16-minute treadmill walk showed 0.66 miles, 65 active calories, 97 total calories, 32 feet of elevation gain, and a 115 BPM average heart rate, just like if I’d worn an Apple Watch.

I had been getting the impression that gym equipment manufacturers had been abandoning GymKit support - if they ever had done so initially. I even got the impression that the majority of equipment in Apple's own onsite Gym at the Apple Park may not have supported it - at least originally.

Does Apple have a webpage listing compatible brands and models? Like they do/did for HomeKit.

What is other people perception? Any rowing machines that support it?

…checks - surprisingly it looks like Peloton do support it on their bikes.

If I tried to use GymKit on iPhone without AirPods, the iPhone disconnected when the workout started because it had no heart-rate source. If I tried to start GymKit from iPhone while wearing Apple Watch, iOS pointed me back to the Workout app on Apple Watch instead, though you can continue without using the watch.

AirPods heart-rate permission also matters. You can manage it in Settings under your AirPods settings and privacy options. I had turned it off, mostly as a theoretical battery-saving move, but this test convinced me to turn it back on. AirPods Pro 3 can also work with Apple Watch to provide the best available heart-rate data.

It has been revealed that gymKit on iPhone is one of those iOS 27 features that sounds small until it solves a real problem. If Apple Watch is your default workout tracker, it probably stays that way.

But if your watch dies or you forget it at home, iPhone plus AirPods Pro 3 can now log a treadmill workout with real heart-rate data and real treadmill metrics.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that game consoles are obviously more expensive than they used to be, even when they came out years ago.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Getting your gaming gear fix during the holiday shopping season is an annual tradition, but it’s more crucial this year than ever. The RAM shortage has driven up all electronics prices, right when the biggest game of all time arrives after a 13-year wait. So any discount you can score can have a massive impact on your wallet. Before the main event starts, you can get started with some early Black Friday gaming deals here.

Industry observers note that game consoles are obviously more expensive than they used to be, even when they came out years ago. But bundle deals are still some of the best way to shave some cash off the sticker price. We’ve also got some deals on accessories, which aren’t always hit quite as hard by the component shortage, so there’s more room for savings.

Sources indicate that well, let’s get the bad news out of the way up front: There probably won’t be that many deals on console hardware. Certain retailers might offer discounts on bundles, but given the price increases over the last year, and the already-high demand, your best bet for those is likely checking individual retailers close to you.

Recent findings suggest that nintendo’s the only major outlier, with a discounted Switch 2 with Mario Kart World bundle for $500, or $50 off the normal retail price. That deal will be live now through Dec. 5. You can also pick up a Switch 2 bundle with Switch Sports Resort for $530. If you’re still interested in VR, you can also pick up a Meta Quest 3S bundle for $298 ($52 off) through Saturday.

PC gaming is just as susceptible to the component shortage as consoles, but since there’s a wider range of models, it’s a bit easier to find deals on individual units.

HP Omen Max 16 gaming laptop with AMD Ryzen 7 350 CPU, 32GB DDR5 RAM, RTX 5070 GPU, and 2TB SSD: $2,184 (was $2,649).

Lenovo Legion 5a gaming laptop with AMD Ryzen 7 250 CPU, 32GB DDR5 RAM, RTX 5060 GPU, and 1TB SSD: $1,700 (was $1,999).

Acer Nitro V gaming laptop with Intel Core 7 240H CPU, 16GB DDR5 RAM, RTX 5050 GPU, and 1TB SSD: $1,445 (was $1,700).

MSI Cyborg gaming laptop with Intel Core i5-13420H CPU, 16GB DDR5 RAM, RTX 5050 GPU, 512GB SSD: $943 (was $1,299).

Alienware Aurora gaming desktop with Intel Core Ultra 7 CPU, 32GB DDR5 RAM, RTX 5070 GPU, and 2TB SSD: $2,328 (was $2,628).

Recent findings suggest that the Nintendo Switch and its successor are in a class by themselves, but the consoles kicked off a renaissance of handheld gaming that the rest of the market is still trying to catch up with. Unfortunately, the second-best handheld, the Valve Steam Deck, doesn’t have any Black Friday deals this year. (Unless you count the possibility of another future price increase as a deal.).

However, there are a few gaming handhelds that are getting discounts. Maybe even some you can install SteamOS on yourself. Here are the deals I’ve found so far.

Lenovo Legion Go S (16GB RAM, 512GB SSD) with SteamOS for $750 (was $990).

Lenovo Legion Go S (32GB RAM, 1TB SSD) with SteamOS for $901 (was $1,400).

MSI Claw 8 A2VM (32GB RAM, 1TB SSD) with Windows for $1,000 (was $1,300).

Retropian Color retro handheld for $65 (was $119).

In a recent development, iOS 27.3 is coming soon, and it’s a significant update for upcoming iPhone features, including additions that span six built-in Apple apps. Here’s what’s new.

Apple Music adds a pair of upgrades in iOS 27.3. Selfie Sing is an all-new feature that lets you record short videos of yourself singing along to your favorite songs, aided by onscreen lyrics. It’s perfect for sharing on TikTok or other social platforms.

According to recent reports, if you’re not the type to share karaoke videos online, another nice iOS 27.3 change is that the lyrics view for songs has gotten an iPhone Duo-inspired upgrade in landscape mode. Now, artwork for the song you’re listening to blends beautifully into the stream of lyrics.

Read more: iOS 27.3 upgrades Apple Music in two ways, here’s what’s new.

Safari is getting several exciting latest features in iOS 27.3, including:.

Read more: iOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3 add Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and more to Safari.

Apple’s Health app gets a major overhaul in iOS 27.3, though only for Apple Intelligence-compatible iPhones.

The fresh Health app has an Insights tab for personalized data visualization and guidance, Longevity tab for tracking your health age, and there are new features like educational videos, movement evaluations, and the ability to order labs that get automatically imported into the app.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds all-newly introduced Apple Health app, details here.

Vertical video is coming with a upcoming Clips feature that lets you browse short samples of Apple TV indicates and movies in a TikTok-style vertically scrolling format.

Video podcasts are also coming to the TV app, with the option to automatically sync playback from Apple Podcasts inside the TV app.

Read more: iOS 27.3 brings vertical video and video podcasts to Apple TV app.

Apple Fitness+ is getting a big expansion in iOS 27.3 with a new Gym Strength program.

Sources indicate that gym Strength lets you build a strength program that fits your schedule and the equipment you have on hand. It’s fully customizable and provides Apple’s best offering yet for traditional strength training.

Whether you’re brand newly introduced to strength training or just benefit from some additional structure, Gym Strength is a great reason to try out Fitness+.

Read more: Apple introduces Fitness+ Gym Strength program with personalized workout plans.

Apple’s Freeform app gets a handful of improvements in iOS 27.3, including new text styling options and preset background colors to choose from. You can also generate custom shapes using Apple Intelligence.

Which new iOS 27.3 features are you most excited about? Let us know in the comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that retailers and brands are churning out early Black Friday deals already, including the likes of Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, Samsung, and others. If you're waiting around for Friday, Nov. 27 to do all of your shopping, you might miss out on some deals and unnecessarily make the day more stressful than it needs to be. If you're a Sam's Club member, you have access to many early Black Friday deals worth checking out. I spent some time combing through their website and rounded up my favorite tech deals below.

According to recent reports, the Bose SoundLink Flex SE is a portable Bluetooth speaker with an IP67 waterproof rating. The speaker even floats in the water, so you can bring it with you into the pool. While it doesn't offer full EQ customization in its companion app, the sound has rich bass depth and clear highs out of the box. It also features a speakerphone, allowing you to take calls and speak with it. It's light and portable, and the Bluetooth 5.3 supports multipoint connectivity and SBC, AAC, and aptX codecs. You can get the Bose 2nd Generation SoundLink Flex SE for $89 (originally $139).

Skullcandy makes fun speakers and headphones, although they're not designed for audiophiles (their sound signature is very bass-heavy). Their Skullcandy Stomp XL Max is their attempt at making a portable party speaker. It comes with two wireless mics, making it a great option for karaoke. It holds 12 hours of battery life (up to 20 hours with certain settings), has an IPX5 water resistance rating, and has LED lights that sync to the music. You can get it for $99 (originally $199).

Getting a soundbar can exponentially improve anyone's entertainment system, but a 5.1 system with rear speakers and a subwoofer takes it to the next level. The Samsung HW-Q65F 5.1 Channel Soundbar is $299 (originally $399), and it's a wireless setup that will keep the harmony of "too many cables" in the house. It supports Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X to give you a 3D audio feel, and it has a dialogue feature that will let you hear the whispers.

These kinds of sales are always a good time to upgrade laptops. If you're looking for a powerful computer that is well-rounded, consider the 16-inch HP OmniBook 7 Flip going for $699 (originally $899). This laptop comes with an Intel Ultra 5 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 16GB of RAM (which, honestly, is the minimum anyone should be buying in 2026).

If you need a bigger screen, the 17.3-inch HP OmniBook 3 is a good choice for a bit less money at $649 (originally $999). It comes with an Intel Core Ultra 7 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 12GB of RAM. Part of the bigger screen means a bigger keyboard, so if you deal with numbers a lot, you'd likely appreciate the numeric pad.

In a recent development, if you want your laptop strictly for gaming, the ASUS TUF F16 Gaming laptop is $1,149 (originally $1,399). With an Intel Core 7 processor and the RTX 5060 graphics card, you'll be well set up to tackle heavy games. It comes with a 165Hz refresh rate, Advanced Arc Flow fans and vents to keep your machine cool, and 16GB DDR5 RAM to keep your loads short.

Recent findings suggest that gaming monitors can get expensive promptly, but you can get decent options on a budget. A great example is the 31.5-inch MSi gaming monitor selling for $129 (originally $179). It has a 250Hz refresh rate and a 1ms response time to make gaming smoother. There's also AMD FreeSync Premium to get rid of tearing and stuttering.

Recent findings suggest that budget TVs get substantial discounts during Black Friday, and the 58-inch Vizio QLED TV is one of them. You can get one for $178 (originally $298), and it supports Dolby Vision HDR for better color and contrast. The operating system is the Vizio OS, but of course, you can always change it with a TV dongle if you prefer a different one.

Recent findings suggest that if you prefer to splurge for a better QLED but still get a good deal, the 65-inch Samsung QN90H QLED TV at $1,197.99 (originally $1,497.99) is a great option. It upscales lower-resolution pictures to 4K with AI. It works for gaming with its 144Hz refresh rate, and because the operating system is Tizen OS, it comes with Samsung TV Plus, which brings over 2,700 free channels. The TV also comes with Dolby Atmos, so you can hear audio with a 3D effect as the audio follows objects around the display.

Sources indicate that A 100-inch TV makes a statement: You take your entertainment system seriously. The 100-inch Vizio QLED TV is a budget-friendly option with a $300 discount, at the moment going for $1,198 (originally $1,498). This TV supports Dolby Vision HDR for more vivid images and has hundreds of free channels with the Vizio OS.

According to recent reports, nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Recent findings suggest that sam Club's 2026 Black Friday sale runs from November 26 to November 29, 2026, starting online at 12:01 a.m. on Thanksgiving Day, but the deals start even earlier.

Yes, you'll need to be a member to get the deals, but you can shop online without a membership with a 10% surcharge. However, you can always get a year membership for $120, which includes a Walmart+ membership, free shipping, and other perks.

Sam's Club seems to have more TV deals than Walmart, but Walmart usually has the best deals for budget TVs. Depending on what you're looking for, one might be better than the other.

According to recent reports, starting Nov. 22 through Dec. 5, you can pick up Nintendo's Switch 2 Mario Kart bundle for $499.00, down $50 from $549.99. That includes the console, a download of Mario Kart World, and a 90-day Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership.

If you already have a Switch 2 console and/or Mario Kart World, you're not left out of the Black Friday deals here. From Nov. 22 through Nov. 29, Nintendo is also running discounts on several high-profile Switch and Switch 2 games:.

Donkey Kong Bananza was one of Nintendo's launch titles for the Switch 2. And while it's been out for over a year, Donkey Kong's first 3D game is still among the best-reviewed titles on the console. Nintendo is taking $20 off the game's MSRP for this promotion.

Kirby Air Riders on Switch 2 is only the second installment in the series. The original released all the way back on the GameCube, and while the title typically runs for $69.99, Nintendo is letting it go for $49.99.

Industry observers note that metroid Prime 4 arrived last year after an 18-year wait from Metroid Prime 3: Corruption. The game typically retails for $69.99 for a physical copy on Switch 2, but Nintendo is selling it for $49 during its early Black Friday promotion.

In a recent development, super Mario Galaxy (both the original and the sequel) are beloved by fans. These titles originally released on the Wii, and Nintendo rereleased both for the Switch. (The manufacturer offers a free upgrade to the Switch 2 edition.) Nintendo asks $69.99 for this combo, and while you can find it for under $60, you'll officially be able to pick it up for $48.97 before Black Friday.

It has been revealed that nintendo's latest Mario Party, Jamboree, has a Switch 2 edition with a rather staggering MSRP of $79.99. While it's the version of the game with the most features, it's also the most expensive. You'll be able to buy it for $39.99 for Black Friday, saving up to $40.

Nintendo rarely offers official discounts on some of its biggest titles, especially in this current era. In addition, Nintendo announced a sale on its digital store that runs from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2, though it didn't say which titles would be on sale. Just keep an eye on all these dates: The Switch 2 console promotion runs longer than the physical and digital games discounts, while the digital sale runs longer than the physical sale. Nintendo says that these discounts will be available "at select retailers," as well as its brick-and-mortar locations in Newly introduced York and San Francisco. You can also buy the Switch 2 bundle through Nintendo's website.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A song about getting ditched for a Texas woman might be leading the charts right now, but, 30 years ago, Deana Carter was offering a different take on romance: the enduring, nostalgic ache of that first love. Or, if we’re being a little less polite, losing your virginity to a college guy next to a river.

The Matraca Berg and Gary Harrison-written hit “Strawberry Wine” went to Number One on country radio in November 1996, and was a seminal part of a female-dominated wave where the genre’s women could push the boundaries of what exactly they were singing about, and how they were singing it. It still resonates.

It has been revealed that A softly-delivered ballad, “Strawberry Wine” wasn’t as outwardly bold as songs like Loretta Lynn’s “Rated X,” or deeply topical like Dolly Parton’s “Down From Dover.” Instead, it’s a wistful reflection on a teen girl’s first love, with a hair of melancholy — and how thinking back on pangs of pleasure can hit as deep in the gut as a good country song. Carter never specifically details exactly what happened between her and this summer fling, but it’s pretty clear what she’s talking about: “love growin’ wild,” “the loss of my innocence,” intoxication, being plucked from the vine before entirely ripening.

As the first single from her album with the equally boundary pushing title Did I Shave My Legs for This, Carter offered a quiet, cheeky reclamation of how subtly or overtly women could sing about sex. And not just sex: sex that comes before, and has nothing to do with, marriage or domestic life, completely devoid of the male gaze.

Carter was 30 when “Strawberry Wine” became a hit, later in life as far as the industry standards for women generally go. A Nashville native, she grew up around music through the eyes of her father, guitarist Fred Carter Jr., who appeared on records by Bob Dylan, Simon & Garfunkel, and Willie Nelson. Carter wrote most of the songs on her debut, but found that “Strawberry Wine” “just nailed my life story, which ended up being everyone’s first experience [with love],” she mentioned in an interview for CMA’s ‘90s Country Forever. She was particularly drawn to the work of Berg, one of the genre’s strongest and boldest talents, unafraid to pitch songs about female experiences to women willing to sing them. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

And Carter was the only one open to taking that risk. Artists like Trisha Yearwood, among many others, reportedly passed on “Strawberry Wine.” But Carter was willing to give a ballad about youthful carnality a go.

In a recent development, “It’s a five-minute waltz about… ya know,” Berg told Rolling Stone. “Deana was a brand-newly introduced artist and she wanted it as her first single. That shocked me. She was a friend of mine, so I was trying to talk her out of it because I wanted her to do well.” Shockingly enough, it did: the song hit Number One at country radio, a rarity for ballad sung by a woman, and went on to inspire others like Kelsea Ballerini, Elizabeth Cook, Ashley McBryde, and Mickey Guyton, who even shouted out “Strawberry Wine” in her song “Rosé” (so did Kid Rock, but we don’t need to mention that one).

Sources indicate that cook, who was motivated to pursue music thanks to Carter’s songs, also referenced it in “Two Chords and a Lie.” “She knows the words to ‘Strawberry Wine’ / It’s a friendly reminder of how love is blind,” Cook sings, in one of dozens of country songs that call out Carter’s hit. These days, country has been racier than ever. From Kacey Musgraves’ washing machine, to Lainey Wilson’s steamy fresh single “Just a Woman,” the influence of Carter and “Strawberry Wine” holds strong. Wilson even once recorded a mashup of her very “Strawberry Wine- inspired “Watermelon Moonshine” on social media, the two hits intertwining.

Industry observers note that “I was definitely channeling ‘Strawberry Wine.’ There will never be another one, but this is kind of my version of that,” Wilson told Variety. “I think songs like that, that are nostalgic like that, they’re just timeless. People can relate. They want to go back to that place; everybody wants to feel at home.”.

Pinocchio at 200: a tale of hunger, greed and Italy's culinary history

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1102 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Repubblica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thirty-five red mullet with tomato sauce, four portions of tripe Parmesan-style and, because the seasoning was not quite satisfactory, three further requests for butter and cheese: this is the Cat's rather frugal dinner at the Red Lobster Inn, justified by a serious stomach complaint.
  • The Fox, evidently in better health, orders a "very light side dish of fattened pullets and young cockerels", followed by a cibreino made with partridges, grey partridges, rabbits and frogs.
  • Pinocchio, who is supposed to be the guest of honour, makes do with "a quarter of a walnut and a crust of bread".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thirty-five red mullet with tomato sauce, four portions of tripe Parmesan-style and, because the seasoning was not quite satisfactory, three further requests for butter and cheese: this is the Cat's rather frugal dinner at the Red Lobster Inn, justified by a serious stomach complaint.

The Fox, evidently in better health, orders a "very light side dish of fattened pullets and young cockerels", followed by a cibreino made with partridges, grey partridges, rabbits and frogs.

Pinocchio, who is supposed to be the guest of honour, makes do with "a quarter of a walnut and a crust of bread". Naturally, he will be the one left to pay the bill.

It would be hard to find a more revealing menu with which to describe 19th-century Italy — and perhaps not just that period.

It has been revealed that in the journey of the puppet who longs to become a real boy, growing up, taking responsibility and learning the difficult art of freedom are all shaped by encounters such as these. Learning how the world works also means discovering that, while everyone gets hungry, not everyone has the same chance to eat their fill.

Meanwhile, the ingredients, dishes and regional references scattered throughout The Adventures of Pinocchio make it one of the most unexpected culinary catalogues in Italian literature.

The cibreino, for a start, deserves a closer look. A traditional Tuscan dish, it is a rich preparation of chicken giblets, combs, livers and other offal, bound together with egg yolk and lemon.

In a recent development, it belongs to a culinary tradition capable of transforming the less prized parts of an animal into a refined dish. The Fox orders a decidedly fanciful version, packed with game and small animals, almost as if to demonstrate that even gluttony requires a certain gastronomic imagination.

The Cat's red mullet, served with tomato sauce, takes us instead towards the Tyrrhenian coast and the cooking of Livorno.

Fish appears again later, when the Green Fisherman prepares to fry Pinocchio alongside hake, grey mullet, sole and anchovies. First he coats them in flour, then drops them into boiling oil: an impeccable procedure, at least from a culinary point of view.

He even offers the puppet a choice: "Would you like to be fried in a pan, or would you prefer to be cooked in a saucepan with tomato sauce?".

Recent findings suggest that pinocchio Goes to School (1911), illustration by Attilio Mussino for Carlo Collodi’s The Adventures of Pinocchio, first published in 1883. (Photo: Fine Art Images/Heritage Images/Getty Images).

Carlo Collodi, born Carlo Lorenzini in Florence on 24 November 1826, must have known a thing or two about food.

His father, Domenico, worked as a cook for the Ginori marquises, giving the future writer an insight into the world of kitchens and pantries that separated aristocratic dining rooms from the tables of ordinary people.

It has been revealed that A patriot, journalist and satirical writer, Collodi also possessed a particular talent for observing human weaknesses. After all, people's characters reveal themselves with remarkable honesty around the dinner table.

In 1883, when The Adventures of Pinocchio was published as a book, Pellegrino Artusi had yet to publish Science in the Kitchen and the Art of Eating Well, which would appear in 1891.

The two books emerged just a few years apart, in the same city, Florence, and seem to tell, each in its own way, the story of the difficult construction of a national identity.

Artusi brought together regional recipes and traditions in a shared language; Collodi sent a puppet travelling through an Italy still deeply divided by economic circumstances and everyday habits.

The novel features tortellini from Bologna, Milanese risotto, Neapolitan macaroni, roast pigeons, chicken breasts and even capon galantine.

The last of these, in Artusi's cookbook, is a small feat of culinary engineering: the bird is deboned, stuffed, cooked in broth and served cold, often accompanied by aspic.

It is a dish requiring time, money and familiarity with the kitchens of grand houses. Nothing could be further removed from Geppetto's humble home.

There, the menu changes radically.

Breakfast consists of three pears, which the carpenter has saved for himself but gives to his hungry son. Pinocchio insists that they be peeled, only to devour the skins and cores as well.

It is one of the book's most delicious scenes: what the puppet initially rejects out of childish whim suddenly becomes desirable when hunger takes hold.

And hunger accompanies Pinocchio from his earliest adventures.

When he finds an egg, he imagines all the ways he might prepare it: as an omelette, cooked on a plate or in a little frying pan, sunny-side up or even swallowed raw. In just a few moments, Collodi offers a miniature treatise on cooking eggs.

But as soon as Pinocchio breaks the shell, a chick emerges, politely says goodbye and walks away.

Food multiplies in his imagination, promises happiness and then disappears.

Consider the wonders prepared by the Blue Fairy.

To celebrate the puppet's upcoming diligence, 200 cups of milky coffee and 400 bread rolls buttered inside and out are laid out.

Elsewhere, there are candied fruits, cakes, panettone, almond sweets, large wafers with cream, sweet liqueurs and alchermes, the traditional Italian red liqueur.

A child's imagination transforms the world into an enormous confectioner's shop.

But the Fairy also understands the value of a simple vegetable. In the Land of the Busy Bees, where everyone works, she offers Pinocchio a plain plate of cauliflower dressed with oil and vinegar.

The novel constantly reverses the relationship between those who eat and those who are eaten.

The enormous whale swallows Geppetto and his son, but inadvertently provides the carpenter with a stock of provisions that allows him to survive.

Tinned meat, ship's biscuits, wine, raisins, cheese, coffee and sugar all come from a vessel swallowed by the monster.

Inside the creature's belly survives an entire collection of 19th-century food-preservation techniques, while the modern world enters the fairy tale through the supplies of a ship.

On the bicentenary of Collodi's birth, rereading Pinocchio through food means rediscovering an Italy — indeed, a world — in which capon galantine and a pot of beans belonged to vastly different lives, and a child might know the names of countless dishes without ever having tasted a single one.

At the Red Lobster Inn, after all, the Cat and the Fox have already grasped a rule that, unfortunately, still works remarkably well: sometimes, all you need to eat your fill is to find someone willing to pick up the bill.

These mini, travel-size containers include eight wipes each — ideal for the office, music festivals, day trips, or your dopp kit while traveling. Get a pack of six (48 wipes total) for $5 at Walmart.

No matter which Dude Wipes you choose this holiday season — the festive “Dingle Bells” wipes or the Pocket Packs — your rear and your plumbing will be in good hand(s). They’re also dermatologically tested and soaked with soothing vitamin E and aloe, which makes them great for sensitive skin. Plus, they’re larger than a standard sheet of toilet paper for all your full-coverage needs.

I finally tested Smeg’s retro-style espresso machine — and it’s the first one I’ve reviewed capable of making cold brew that’s actually cold

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2142 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, looking for a coffee machine to see you through all twelve months of the year (and then some)?
  • Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you.
  • According to recent reports, what do you look for when shopping for an espresso machine?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, looking for a coffee machine to see you through all twelve months of the year (and then some)? The Smeg Espresso & Cold Brew Machine might just scratch that itch. This aesthetically pleasing machine can make genuinely cold cold brew — no lukewarm extraction here — and delicious, hot espresso. Although it's quite expensive in the U.S., it could be an ideal first machine for the budding enthusiast.

Weighty, high-quality accessories.

Extremely expensive in the U.S.

Steam wand takes a while to heat up.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

According to recent reports, what do you look for when shopping for an espresso machine? Function? Coffee-snob-approved features? Affordability? Or style? If it’s the latter, may I introduce you to the Smeg ECF03 — one of the most aesthetically pleasing espresso machines I’ve ever seen?

Also called the Smeg Espresso & Cold Brew Machine, the ECF03 combines Smeg’s trademark ‘50s design with some seriously impressive functionality. The machine makes genuinely cold cold brew — not lukewarm like De’Longhi — and delicious espresso. While the steam wand takes a while to heat up and requires some patience for back-to-back shots, it’s a fun little machine for newbies.

According to recent reports, however, its MSRP isn’t a fun little price tag for newbies — in the U.S., it’ll set you back $699. In the U.K. you can grab it for as low as £204. No, that’s not a typo. £204. So, is this enough to make it one of the best espresso machines? To find out, you’ll need to keep reading this Smeg ECF03 review.

Single shot portafilter (single-walled and dual-walled), double shot portafilter (single-walled and dual-walled), tamper, cleaning disc, brush, cleaning needle.

It has been revealed that the Smeg ECF03 is outrageously expensive in the U.S., and pretty par for the course in the U.K. On the east side of the Atlantic, you’re looking at $699 from Amazon, but over on the west, you’ll only pay £399 at John Lewis. It’s also on clearance at Curry’s for £204, which is utterly bizarre, seeing as this machine only came out last year, but I’d recommend buying there if you’re fast. I’m not sure how long that sale price will last as I write this.

In the U.S., this machine is really overpriced. $699 for a Thermoblock espresso machine with no grinder is steep. For $699, you can get the Breville Barista Express or the Breville Bambino Plus with the Baratza Encore ESP grinder.

You can also get the De’Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo for $699, which has a built-in grinder, and the Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini for $449 — which also has a built-in grinder.

See what I mean? You’d still have to buy a grinder separately to make the most of the ECF03. That’s an extra $200. An MSRP of around $400-$500 would have made more sense, putting the ECF03 in line with the best entry-level espresso machines, Breville Bambino Plus and Breville Bambino ($299).

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Sources indicate that of course, the ECF03 can make cold brew, so you wouldn’t need to purchase a separate cold brew maker or French press for cold brew, but I’m not sure this is worth the extra $200-$300 over Breville’s options. On top of that, the aforementioned De’Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo can make “cold brew” for the same price.

I use quotation marks because De’Longhi’s cold brew comes out warm — but I’ll get into that later.

While the ECF03 has a 58mm portafilter — closer to the specialty coffee commercial standard than Breville’s 54mm — I’m not sure that’s worth the extra $$$.

The ECF03 looks like (almost) everything Smeg makes: retro, stylish, and oh-so cool. The only machine to forgo the trademark Smeg aesthetic is the $1,599 Semi-Professional/Mini Pro/EMC02 (the many-monikered machine), which was a collaboration between Smeg and La Pavoni.

If you like the Smeg aesthetic, you’ll be pleased. If it’s not your cup of tea, you won’t be pleased. It’s as simple as that.

For a $699 machine, though, the ECF03 is a touch more plasticky than I’d like. That gorgeous white chassis? Shiny plastic. The steam wand knob also feels like plastic. If it’s not actually plastic, color me surprised, but it sure does look and feel like it.

There’s a manometer, which is a nice touch, but it doesn’t actually show the specific bar pressure of each step. I assume anything in the perforated section on the bottom right means over 9 bars, but I’d like numbers on the next iteration of this machine.

Industry observers note that but the accessories. Oh, the accessories. They’re beautiful. The 58mm tamper is super weighty, making it feel incredibly high quality, and the 58mm portafilter is just as professional. They actually feel like weapons. This is the mark of a high-quality machine. If you unbox a $500+ espresso machine and the tamper is plastic, run. Run fast.

Naturally, you get a pressurized (dual-wall) and non-pressurized (single-wall) portafilter basket. I only used the single-wall one as I have the best grinder in the world, Mazzer Philos, so I didn’t need to resort to the help-I’ve-used-pre-ground-coffee-and-now-my-espresso-tastes-bad dual-walled portafilters.

The Smeg ECF03 makes delicious espresso. As mentioned earlier, I used the non-pressurized portafilters and fresh Ethiopian beans ground on my Mazzer Philos. I recommend you also use freshly ground coffee and the non-pressurized portafilters for the best experience. Pressurized portafilters can destroy nuance and delicate flavors in specialty coffee beans, but are fine for pre-ground coffee if that’s what you like.

Sources indicate that to make espresso, I ground 18g of my Ethiopian coffee beans to click 25 on the Philos, which is coarser than the Fellow Espresso Series 1’s ($1,499) optimal grind size, but similar to the Breville Bambino’s ideal range of 22-25. For context, I use the same coffee beans for every single machine.

Sources indicate that here’s a photo of a “perfect” espresso. This extracted 35.6g in 26 seconds, which is in the “golden window” of espresso extraction.

Industry observers note that as you can see, there’s a lovely crema on top, with a delicate, fluffy texture and a nice color to the shot. While this might not impress serious espresso enthusiasts — the shot was a little bitter at the end of the mouthful — it’s definitely fine if you are less of a hobbyist and more of an appreciator.

Sources indicate that overall, the espresso tastes very Italian. Strong-bodied, rich, and dark, even when using medium-roasted beans. Again, if you’re an espresso enthusiast, you might want to invest a little more in the Fellow Espresso Series 1 or Lelit Mara X3 ($1,999) — or the Smeg EMC02, which I still dream about.

As an integral part of this machine’s marketing, it’s only logical I discuss cold brew in detail. You access cold brew via the “Blue menu”, which is activated by pressing the power button while the machine is already switched on. The buttons will glow blue, meaning you’re in cold brew mode.

Recent findings suggest that according to the manual, you’re supposed to use “one or two” ice cubes per cold brew, but I ignored that. I filled my cup about halfway with ice cubes, dosed 18g of medium-fine ground coffee in the non-pressurized portafilter basket, and set it to pull a double shot of cold brew. Not sure how you can get a “double shot” of cold brew, but I assume that’s just the machine’s limited button options.

The cold brew took four minutes and fifty-three seconds to fill my glass. The machine is programmed to dose a certain volume of cold brew, but I used a 12-ounce glass filled with ice, so I didn’t need the “whole” serving.

Here’s a photo of stated cold brew.

Industry observers note that as you can see, it’s relatively dark, with a strong body. The ice cubes aren’t all melted — can you guess what that means? Yes, it actually brews cold! This is fantastic news; De’Longhi machines tend to brew lukewarm, or sometimes even actively warm cold brew (which then requires ice to make it cold).

In a recent development, as for the taste, this cold brew was fine. I wouldn’t throw away my Espro P7 French press, which I use to make cold brew the traditional way (16 hours at room temperature), but I also wouldn’t turn my nose up at rapid cold brew from the Smeg. I think this will do if you want a cold coffee in a pinch, but serious cold brew lovers need not apply.

According to recent reports, while the ECF03 makes a delicious espresso, its steam wand isn’t as powerful as I’d like it to be. Don’t get me wrong, this is nowhere near as egregious as machines like the Casabrews Ultra ($349), but for $699, I’d expect at least a Bambino Plus-level wand.

Recent findings suggest that I was able to get perfect microfoam, but it took a while to steam an 8oz jug — around a minute. Here’s a photo of a flat white I made on the ECF03.

As you can see, the milk texture is perfect, with smooth, almost melted-marshmallow texture. There are zero bubbles and the milk is extremely creamy. This tasted divine.

Sources indicate that however, it’s worth noting that I’m an ex-professional barista and an espresso machine tester of almost three years. I have a lot of practice. If this is your first espresso machine, you will need to baby that steam wand. Because it’s lower pressure than the Breville Bambino/Bambino Plus, you’ll need to learn how to eke out delicate texture even when you can’t achieve the perfect vortex.

At 14.3 x 8.1 x 11.6 inches, the ECF03 isn’t the smallest, nor the largest, espresso machine I’ve tested. As it has no grinder, you’ll need a separate one, so I recommend making sure you’ve got enough to room for both the machine and its grinder before purchasing.

The water tank is at the back of the machine, so you’ll need a decent amount of upper-cupboard clearance space — at least 17 inches, I’d say.

Speaking of water tank, Smeg provides you with water hardness strips, but no water filter. If you wanted to filter your water, you’d need to buy that separately. Smeg sells these for $25 on its website, which is pretty disappointing to see considering this machine is already $699.

It has been revealed that when you do need to descale, Smeg doesn’t sell its own descaler. I’d recommend using De’Longhi’s or Durgol’s, which are $19 for 2 bottles and $15 for 4 bottles, respectively.

Industry observers note that last but certainly not least — warranty. Smeg offers a 2-year warranty if purchased from the Smeg store or a 1-year warranty from another outlet. This is pretty disappointing when De’Longhi, Breville, and Ninja all offer 2-year warranties as standard — and many of their machines cost less than the ECF03.

Recent findings suggest that the Smeg ECF03 is ideal for espresso beginners. If you want to feel fancier than, say, a Casabrews (and you have the money to back it up, of course), then by all means you should invest in a Smeg. The ECF03 is really easy to use, makes actually cold cold brew, and has a mostly useful manometer for pressure-watching.

Industry observers note that although the steam wand means you need to really pay attention during milk heating, if you’re willing to put the work in, you’ll get barista-quality coffee out of it. And I mean… just look at it! Everything Smeg makes is an aesthetic marvel, and the ECF03 is no different.

If you’re in the U.K., you’re getting a much better deal, but if you find it on sale in the U.S., I’m sure you won’t be disappointed.

iOS 27 gave your iPhone an alarm feature that’s long been missing

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (388 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5mac

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alarms are one of the most vital iPhone features, and iOS 27 offers a key feature that should help your alarm actually wake you: a newly introduced volume setting for alarms that’s independent of other volume settings.
  • Have you ever accidentally slept through an alarm?
  • I suspect that’s a pretty common reason for missed alarms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alarms are one of the most vital iPhone features, and iOS 27 offers a key feature that should help your alarm actually wake you: a newly introduced volume setting for alarms that’s independent of other volume settings.

Have you ever accidentally slept through an alarm? We’ve all done it. And most often for me, it’s because my alarm volume was unintentionally set to a very low level.

I suspect that’s a pretty common reason for missed alarms. And in iOS 27, Apple finally has the fix—but it requires manually setting up.

Inside Settings ⇾ Sounds & Haptics, you can now set a volume for alarms that’s independent from the systemwide ringtone setting.

Industry observers note that iOS 27 has two new sections in this Settings screen: Alarms and Timers, and Alerts and System Sounds. Both include ‘Match Ringtone Volume’ toggles that are on by default. This means your volume for alarms, timers, alerts, and other system sounds are all determined by the ringtone volume.

But if you disable the Alarms and Timers toggle, you’ll get a newly introduced volume slider that applies only to those system functions, and won’t be impacted by your ringtone volume.

As seen above, this means you can crank the Alarms and Timers volume up to the maximum level without making every other system sound, including notifications and phone calls, be similarly deafening.

So the next time you sleep through your alarm, it won’t be because the alarm was too quiet.

In case you missed it, iOS 26 introduced a welcome feature that lets you set custom snooze durations for alarms, and also an option to have alarms trigger on your iPhone even if you’re wearing an Apple Watch.

Do you strategy to set a custom volume setting for alarms in iOS 27? Let us know in the comments.

Tech Report: Spending 35B Opus 5.5 Tokens to Write a Symphony

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2135 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Danprice

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "I fear not the man the man who one shots 2500 symphonies with Claude, rather I fear the man who 2500 shots a single symphony with Claude".
  • So, I got bored and wanted to push Opus to its limit with respect to music composition.
  • You can watch a full virtual instrument rendering of the composition on youtube here, which is likely higher quality than the version you'd get streamed from x.com:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"I fear not the man the man who one shots 2500 symphonies with Claude, rather I fear the man who 2500 shots a single symphony with Claude".

So, I got bored and wanted to push Opus to its limit with respect to music composition. Basically, I did the meme:.

You can watch a full virtual instrument rendering of the composition on youtube here, which is likely higher quality than the version you'd get streamed from x.com:.

YouTube picks the picture quality from your connection and the size of the player. For a sharper score, choose 1080p or higher under the gear icon, or go full screen.

The source of the scores, the critics' reviews and the scripts are on GitHub: github.com/halfprice06/claude-symphony.

These are virtual instruments, so the audio quality is not as good as if an orchestra recorded this live. But its pretty good, and considering Claude did all of the mockup and rendering in a DAW with pro-level VSTs, I'd say the result is still pretty impressive.

The whole thing used around 35 billion Opus tokens.

Recent findings suggest that we used Claude Code Projects (beta) for this, and I find it really useful for project-based coding. The orchestrator / thread model worked really well for us in practice. Generally, each movement was owned by a thread.

I thought the process I used to achieve this was pretty interesting, so I decided to write it up.

tl;dr - For things that can't be 'verified' as good or bad like art/music, just make the agent do more iterations, way more iterations than you think.

There were three jobs: writing the symphony, turning the score into a recording, and making the video. I'll go through them in that order.

Claude Opus 5.5 composed a four-movement symphony for full orchestra, about 25 minutes of music, in one month. This is how it was done.

Sources indicate that claude cannot easily click notes onto a staff, but it can write text. So the whole score was written in LilyPond, a free program that turns typed text into printed sheet music. A note is a letter and a number: c4 is a C that lasts a quarter note. From the same text, LilyPond also produces a basic computer playback.

Because the score is text, Claude could edit it, compare two versions, and check it with small programs, the way programmers work on code.

In a recent development, these eight bars for the first violins are copied from the score's source text. Point at a note in the text or on the staff to find it in the other. Click a note to hear it.

Swipe the staff sideways to see all of it.

"Only these notes" is a simple synthesizer in your browser playing the violin line alone. The recording is the same eight bars from the final mockup, with the whole orchestra.

Sources indicate that the method is called an actor-critic loop. One Claude, the composer, writes the music. Another Claude, the critic, reviews it.

Each critic looked at one subject only, such as melody, harmony, the use of the instruments, or whether the parts are playable. A written log recorded every decision, so that a later critic would not undo an earlier one.

According to recent reports, each movement went through this loop about 600 times. With four movements, that's about 2,400 rounds.

Industry observers note that originally I only planned to do this looping process around 50 times. But once I hit 50, it seemed like the agent was still improving. So, I just kept going. This entire process was mostly autonomous. I just prompted Claude to keep going.

In a recent development, each square is one round. Time runs from left to right, ten rounds per column, and each of the ten rows is one critic's subject. Pick a square to read that round's line in the log.

Swipe the grid sideways to see later rounds.

the log records a change the log notes nothing was changed These are the real lines from the log, cut to about 200 characters. They are written in the working shorthand of the loop, with bar numbers and instrument names.

This explorer needs JavaScript.

A critic's opinion was not enough. I supplied standard textbooks on orchestration, harmony and music notation. From then on, each critic was assigned a chapter and had to show where the score followed it and where it did not.

In a recent development, one example: an orchestration textbook notes that in loud passages two horns are needed to balance one trumpet. A critic checked every loud brass chord against that rule, found three chords where an important note was too weak, and proposed fixes. The composer accepted all three.

Claude also collected scores by composers such as Beethoven, Dvořák and Tchaikovsky. Every tenth critic compared a whole movement with one movement by a master and answered one question: would a conductor believe a master wrote this?

It has been revealed that I set the goal: a symphony that could pass for the work of a master, with melodies people remember. I chose the method, supplied the books and decided how long the loops ran. I left the musical choices to Claude.

Recent findings suggest that I was also the only one who could listen. Claude cannot hear audio, so it judged the music from the written score. I listened to computer playbacks and asked for a small number of changes.

According to recent reports, I thought it would be neat to compare version 1 of each movement against the final version. There are no high quality recordings of version 1, so both are played here with the same basic MIDI sounds, which is the closest thing to compare.

According to recent reports, the strip is the final version of the movement, one segment per bar. The brighter a bar, the more of its notes are new or changed since version 1. Click anywhere on the strip to play from that bar, and switch between the two versions while it plays.

A note counts as kept when version 1 has the same pitch at the same place in the matching bar. A pitch played by several instruments at once counts once. A program matched the bars of the two versions, so the shading is approximate. Both versions are set to the same volume.

This comparison needs JavaScript.

Version 1 of Movement I was a sketch for strings only, and its first theme was different. In Movements II, III and IV the main themes begin with the same notes in version 1 and in the final version, and the bright bars on the strips show where the changes are. By the count described above, about 14% of the notes in the final Movement I were already in version 1, 35% in Movement II, 61% in Movement III and 55% in Movement IV.

Claude wrote 99.9% of every single element of the composition. I maybe influenced a measure or two of note selection over the whole process.

A written score doesn't make any sound, so the next job was a recording.

The recordings of the symphony are not a live orchestra. They are mockups: every note was recorded in advance by real players, and software plays those recordings back in the order the score asks for. This is how the four mockups, about 25 minutes of music, were made.

According to recent reports, two programs did the work, both on my Mac. REAPER is a music production program. It holds one track per instrument, mixes them together and saves the result as an audio file. EastWest Hollywood Orchestra is the library of recorded notes. (These are the DAW and the pro-level VSTs I mentioned at the top.).

Claude did not click around in either program. It wrote scripts that read the score and built each REAPER project from it. The score is a text file, written in LilyPond, so a script can read every note and every marking directly.

A person making a mockup listens, adjusts, and listens again. Claude cannot listen. It can only measure the audio file. So after every recording it checked things that can be measured:.

Sources indicate that each movement was improved in rounds. Every round had the same four steps:.

The four movements took 184 rounds in total.

Industry observers note that the same 18 bars, from the basic computer playback to the final recording. Pick a stage to hear it. You can switch while it plays.

All six clips are set to the same volume here, so the differences you hear are in the playing and the mix. As first made, rounds 0 to 11 were 5 to 6 dB quieter than rounds 20 and 30.

According to recent reports, the measurements missed things, and I caught them by listening. I said the long timpani rolls were drowning out other instruments. I said the accents were too harsh, the sound was "too wet" and "a bit mushy", repeated notes were hard to tell apart, and the recordings were too quiet on AirPods.

Recent findings suggest that each of my notes became a rule, and a new thing for the critics to measure. Two examples:.

In a recent development, about a month in, we studied how professionals make mockups. The sources were YouTube tutorials by film-score mixers, the sample library maker's own template project, and project files that composers have shared for others to study. Three lessons changed the recordings most: use less reverb, shape each phrase so it rises and falls, and leave a small gap between repeated notes.

The last job was the video at the YouTube link above.

Sources indicate that each video demonstrates the orchestra's sheet music as a dark page. Every note lights up at the moment it sounds, in a color for its instrument, and a small light hops from note to note along each instrument's line. A program worked all of this out from the written score and the recording.

Recent findings suggest that like I remarked above, the score is written as text in LilyPond. For the videos, LilyPond printed each movement as one long line and also wrote down where on the page it put every note. That gave the video program the exact place of all 22,979 notes.

The recording speeds up and slows down, as any performance does. REAPER, the software that made the recording, keeps a list of every change of speed. The video program uses that list to work out the second at which each note sounds. The lights land within two hundredths of a second of the sound.

Sources indicate that an orchestra's score is too tall to fit on the screen, so the camera shows only part of the page. It goes to the instruments that are loudest in the recording at that moment. The program prepares the camera's whole route before it draws anything, so the camera moves seldom and arrives before the passage it is moving to begins. When two instruments far apart on the page matter at the same time, the screen splits in two.

In a recent development, each instrument's name is printed on the page where it starts to play. Short labels, 124 in all, point out what a music theory class would: a theme coming back, an unusual chord, a quotation from an earlier movement. One Claude wrote the labels from the score, and a second Claude checked every one against the notes.

Sources indicate that I watched each version and said what looked wrong. The camera jerked around. The instrument names shifted about. The opening took 19 seconds to reach the first sound. Each comment led to a fix, and the videos were made five times in two days. The four movements were then joined into one 25-minute video for YouTube, and its music now starts in the first second.

So that's the whole process. Add it up and it's about 2,400 rounds on the score, 184 on the recordings and 5 on the video. That's roughly the 2500 in the title.

According to recent reports, none of those rounds had a pass/fail test, because there isn't one for whether music is good. What I could do was give each critic one narrow thing to check, make it back up its opinion with a textbook or a measurement, and run the loop way more times than seemed necessary. Then I listened to the result myself, because Claude can't.

The scores, the reviews and the scripts from this project are on GitHub: github.com/halfprice06/claude-symphony.

If you are with a professional symphony orchestra and might be interested in performing this live, please reach out to me. I'm on X at x.com/gooby_esq, or you can email me at [email protected].

‘All of a Sudden’ Is the Rare Movie That May Change Your Life
