  • It has been revealed that as anyone who’s seen the Oscar winner Drive My Car and Happy Hour — his 2015 magnum opus that clocks in at a little over five hours, and frankly could have sustained itself for twice that running time — will tell you, the Japanese filmmaker can take extended scenes of discussion and turn them into the sort of exchanges that make you lean forward.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we go to the movies for any number of reasons: to laugh, to cry, to care (bless you, Nicole Kidman), to be thrilled or scared or see if Spider-Man makes it out of a scrape with a supervillain alive. The notion that we might be drawn to films so we can listen to other people talk — to be not just voyeurs but eavesdroppers — isn’t usually one of the top reasons for spending a lot of time sitting in the dark and staring at shadows on a screen. It’s a show-don’t-tell medium.

Still, there are a handful of auteurs who excel at making the art of conversation seem everything from enthralling to downright cinematic. Tarantino loves letting his characters digress at length in between violent set pieces and gratuitous shots of feet. The work of French writer-director Eric Rohmer is synonymous with long sequences of people doing nothing more than chatting about intellectual matters great and small. (His work also gave us one of the all-time great 1970’s cine-disses.) If Louis Malle had made nothing but My Dinner With Andre, he’d still be considered canon-worthy. Richard Linklater, Jean Eustache, Whit Stillman — all first-rate movie conversationalists. And then there’s Ryusuke Hamaguchi.

It has been revealed that as anyone who’s seen the Oscar winner Drive My Car and Happy Hour — his 2015 magnum opus that clocks in at a little over five hours, and frankly could have sustained itself for twice that running time — will tell you, the Japanese filmmaker can take extended scenes of discussion and turn them into the sort of exchanges that make you lean forward. If anyone could make a connect-the-dots presentation about capitalism, healthcare, and burnout cycles scrawled onto a whiteboard in real time feel absolutely compelling, it’s him. That happens to be the centerpiece of his latest drama All of a Sudden, an ironic title for a masterwork intent on taking its time and giving its characters plenty of space to ruminate. The end result is all the better for it, too. This is the type of movie that prizes philosophical pursuits over pulse-pounding chases, and the spark of communicating ideas over crass spectacle. It’s admittedly not for everyone. For filmgoers who find two human beings connecting over reflections on life, death, art, and caretaking, however, Hamaguchi’s astounding ode to empathy as an emotional foundation for coexistence is nothing short of manna. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

The person giving that impromptu whiteboard lecture is Mari (Tao Okomoto), a Japanese playwright and theater director who’s mounting one of her productions in Paris. The woman on the receiving end of this Socio-economics 101 lesson is Marie-Lou (Virginia Efira). She is the director of a memory-care facility, overseeing a half-dozen or so patients. Marie-Lou is a staunch advocate for “humanitude,” a four-pillar methodology developed in France for treating those enduring various stages of dementia and Alzheimer’s. (Hamaguchi himself became familiar with this technique when his grandmother was being cared for roughly a decade ago.) The younger members of her staff are slow to adapt to this ideology that emphasizes touch and “verticality” over more traditional treatment plans; the older nurses are flat out refusing to learn it at all. The uphill battle of fighting for what is, in Marie-Lou’s eyes, a more humane way of healthcare is taking its toll on her.

Recent findings suggest that it’s pure coincidence that Marie-Lou happens to meet Mari after an encounter with a developmentally disabled kid (Kodai Kurasaki) and his grandfather (Kyôzô Nagatsuka), who happens to be an actor in Mari’s play. The two hit it off, and after a performance, hang out and talk, talk, talk through the wee small hours. By the time we witness Marie-Lou being schooling on how the world works via whiteboard, you can tell the bond between these two is tight. Lifelong friendships have been forged over less.

In a recent development, hamaguchi is using a 2019 collection of letters between Maho Isono and Makiko Miyano, known in some English editions as You and I: The Illness Got Worse, as a foundation here — which makes All of a Sudden something like an adaptation, and the equivalent of an epistolary movie. Correspondence is king here; it just happens to be occurring face to face instead of one post at a time. Like Isano, Marie-Lou comes from a medical background. And like Miyano, a philosopher by trade, Mari has a tendency to think major thoughts and emphasize the way that the “littlest” people make up (and are at the mercy of) a far bigger picture. It’s worth noting Miyano was diagnosed with terminal cancer when she met her pen pal — a condition that Hamaguchi passes on to Mari as well. Time is something that seems to contract, expand, and often feel like it stops still in the director’s work. But in terms of Mari and Marie-Lou’s story, it’s very much of the essence. Their time together is fleeting, and the last thing they’re taking for granted. Related Content She Cries. She Rages. She Sings Harry Styles. Is Sandra Hüller the MVP of 2026? It Was Butchered Beyond Belief. Now the Most Shocking 1970s Movie Returns as a Masterpiece Taylor Swift to Perform at Academy Museum's Annual Gala ‘NAZA’ Wants You to Bear Witness.

Recent findings suggest that all of a Sudden is filled with languorous side trips, large chunks of stand-alone bits of business, and segments centered around caretaking that almost feel like process movies unto themselves. A performance of Mari’s play is essentially seen in full, then partially reprised near the end. Training sessions and testimonials from family members and loved ones of patients share screen time with our central duo’s chatathons. Anyone squeamish over the idea of a group foot massage (part of the humanitude’s more experimental notions of engagement between facility workers and their wards) may want to leave for popcorn before the film hits its three-hour mark. Mari wants to return to Japan to deal with her illness, so Marie-Lou goes with her. So does the movie. Trending Stories Cher’s Victory in Royalties War Under Fire as Mary Bono Pushes for Reversal Chris Christie to Republicans: ‘I Don’t Want to Hear Your Whining’ Amanda Seyfried Admits She ‘Told a Lot of People’ About Elizabeth Holmes Documentary 50 Years Ago Today: Neil Young Played a 1 A.M. Concert the Morning of the Last Waltz.

Yet Hamaguchi’s not simply letting seemingly tangential events or the daily drudge of work luxuriously play out for their own sake. Every minute is accounted for story-wise, and not a moment is wasted. He’s not painting a portrait so much as a mural, one that keeps its central duo in constant focus even as its generous with its supporting players and peripheral bits of business. We should note that both Efira and Okomoto are equally outstanding, solo and in tandem, and equally adept at holding up their ends of the long conversations that punctuate the filmmaker’s meditations on how one spends what little time they have on this hurling rock in the cosmos. There’s a rapport happening between the two that bypasses cultural backgrounds, different performing styles, separate languages — the dialogue moves back and forth between French and Japanese so fluently that it sometimes takes you a second to realize when switches between tongues. The lingua franca here is a shared understanding of the need for companionship and the joy of communication. Not for nothing did both of them share the Best Actress award at Cannes.

According to recent reports, it’s thrilling to watch what is, at its base, an origin story of a friendship, even if we know it’s a brief one — because we know where this ends. Yet Hamaguchi wants to acknowledge that quality, not quantity, is what matters in terms of togetherness. That applies to the humanism that underlines every thing that’s on screen as well, and that particular quality is in abundance. The movie may seem to drift, to detour, or to determinedly test one’s patience when examining things outside of Mari and Marie-Lou’s rich discussions about the world they live in, and the world they’ll leave behind. Yet All of a Sudden is all of a piece, and makes listening in feel like an honor. Hamaguchi is delivering an eloquent statement about the need for looking after one another in a myriad of different ways, ranging from creativity to giving someone a good farewell. Despite keeping one eye on death, it’s a primer for a possible way to live a good life — and the rare movie that may change yours.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • To use Task, open Gemini and create a new chat.
  • Of course, I did the thing that every AI demo wants you to do: I asked Gemini to create a daily morning briefing for me, highlighting all key emails, calendar appointments, and tasks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that google loves a rebrand. What started off as "Spark" is now "Task" in Gemini—not to be confused with Google Tasks, the to-do app. Google took its Spark AI agent, which used to live in a separate tab, and integrated it into the Gemini interface. Gemini Task is available globally, and it’s completely free to use for some. That stated, some features are limited to the U.S. and, of course, subject to some pretty strict usage limits. While not exactly a replacement for ChatGPT Dots or Meta Muse, you can think of Gemini Task as a controlled version of an AI agent that can do quite a lot in the background.

To use Task, open Gemini and create a new chat. You’ll see a Task tab next to Chat. Switch to it, and start writing your prompt. (You’ll also see some suggested options here.) Type your task or action and press "Send." The feature works best if you’ve already enabled Personal Intelligence on your Google account, and have connected services like Gmail, Google Drive, and Photos as well. You can then tag “@Gmail” to use your Gmail account, or even a third-party connector. Task natively supports automation, so you can say something like, "run this task once every day," and the AI will add it to your Scheduled Tasks section.

Of course, I did the thing that every AI demo wants you to do: I asked Gemini to create a daily morning briefing for me, highlighting all key emails, calendar appointments, and tasks. And, in my experience, it works really well. It reminded me of this article's due date, that I have a couple of pitches in my inbox to review, that a credit card bill is due soon, and that there are some holidays around the corner.

According to recent reports, gemini is very good at retrieving information from emails and taking action. For example, I created an automation that collects all my coffee orders for the month and presents the data in Google Sheets. I then asked Task to create a subscription manager for me. Instead of paying for a third-party app, it took a few minutes to collate the services I pay for into one list. It even accounted for the currency differences (some subscriptions are in USD, some in INR) and gave me a tally in INR, along with things like average monthly cost, and more.

While Gemini can connect to the open web, it's quite a hostile place right now for an AI bot. Websites are blocking agents from accessing their pages, which hinders their effectiveness. I asked Gemini to create a task that monitors the price of the Sony WH-1000XM5 headphones daily. For this, it asked my permission to spin up a remote browser, and loaded up Amazon, only to be blocked instantly. It did succeed in opening Croma though (a national retailer in India), but it took almost a minute for it to figure out that the price had not dropped below what I asked for. Would it be quicker and less resource-intensive if I did this myself? Yes, but the fact that Gemini can do this every evening like clockwork is the real advantage—as long as the websites comply, that is.

If you're going to try Task in Gemini for free, there are some limitations you should know about. The free plan only lets you run tasks once per day, and you can’t be granular about the exact timing. (Paid Gemini intends have no such restrictions.) You can only run 10 tasks at the same time, while the limit is 50 tasks for AI Pro owners. Compute-based usage limits will also apply, based on your plan. The free access is currently live in India, the U.S., Canada, Australia, Japan, and South Korea.

Some features, though, are only for U.S. owners. Gemini’s feature that lets you call businesses on your behalf is restricted to the States, as is the ability to forward emails to [email protected] to automatically turn the contents of the email into a task (like adding a college schedule to your calendar). U.S. users can also connect their Google Wallet account to set up payments at supported stores.

Gemini Task is not a proactive agent, nor is it trying to be. You still have to check the work. You have to approve any key steps, and if a website blocks AI models, there’s not a lot Gemini can do about it. For someone like me, who’s all-in on the Google ecosystem, I do see value in Gemini Task. The deep and robust Gmail integration is worth it alone. If you’re on the free proposal, set up a couple of background tasks related to Gmail, Google Drive, or background research that run every morning, and call it a day. And if you’re paying for AI Pro, you can get a lot more done.

The lawsuit accusing Cardi B and Offset of duping the owner of a Beverly Hills mega-mansion into letting them film a music video for her song “Like What” for a discounted TikTok video rate has been dismissed after the parties reached a confidential settlement, a source and court documents obtained by Rolling Stone reveal.

Recent findings suggest that A source confirmed the parties reached a settlement “subject to confidentiality.” The private pact came after both sides told a judge in April they were open to mediation and just weeks before a trial set to begin Jan. 5. Lawyers for both sides did not provide comment when contacted by Rolling Stone.

When property owner Bi LLC first sued in 2024, it claimed Cardi B, born Belcalis Almánzar, and her estranged husband, whose real name is Kiari Cephus, had their eyes on the striking glass-and-aluminum mansion once occupied by Justin Bieber and “devised a blueprint” to use it “without paying full market value.” The owner alleged the couple’s representatives anonymously booked the mansion “under the false pretense” that it would be used for a TikTok video. Cardi and Offset then showed up and made the property’s “distinctive architecture” the “centerpiece” of a full-length music video, the lawsuit claimed.

It has been revealed that cardi fired back on X, formerly Twitter, the same day the complaint was filed, saying the lawsuit was riddled with inaccuracies. “We paid those people $10,000 IN CASH to rent the property for a whole 24 hours that same day 6am to 6am the next morning and we went over by ONE hour which we paid overage fees to the realtor for in March,” she wrote. The “Money” singer added that the property “had cameras all over” and both the realtors and the owners were present “the ENTIRE time.”.

“I got pics and videos of them on set!! Now they wanna finesse us trying to say we told them it was a TikTok video when that was nowhere in the contract and like they didn’t hear the whole song playing and see how long we was shooting,” she wrote. “Why would it take us 24 hours to shoot a TikTok? The problem is people wanna find loopholes and get over but IRON YOUR BEST SUIT BITCH I’ll see you in court!!!!” Trending Stories Cher’s Victory in Royalties War Under Fire as Mary Bono Pushes for Reversal Chris Christie to Republicans: ‘I Don’t Want to Hear Your Whining’ 50 Years Ago Today: Neil Young Played a 1 A.M. Concert the Morning of the Last Waltz Amanda Seyfried Admits She ‘Told a Lot of People’ About Elizabeth Holmes Documentary.

It has been revealed that her lawyers sought to toss the lawsuit, arguing it failed to state any viable claims, but the judge found sufficient grounds for the case to proceed to discovery. “The complaint adequately alleges that plaintiff justifiably relied to its detriment on defendants’ misrepresentation that the intent was to merely film a TikTok, when in fact defendants filmed a professional music video,” the judge wrote in February 2025.

Latest Update: MagSafe Monday: Anker’s MagGo Pro 2 has a built-in fan to keep 25W Qi2.2 charging from slowing down

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the biggest glitch with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat.
  • MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.
  • Heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the biggest glitch with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat. It doesn’t matter if the battery specs say it can charge at Qi2.2 speeds if the heat slows it down after 15 minutes. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro directly targets heat with a built-in fan in the MagSafe battery.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge. Anker’s answer in the MagGo 2 Pro is a small fan inside of it. Anker states it keeps the charging surface below 96.8°F, and the fan adjusts its speed based on what’s plugged in and how the charge is progressing. You can switch between Cool and Silent modes if you don’t want to hear it running at all.

The result of having this fan is a Qi2.2 power bank that actually reaches Qi2.2 speeds for a full charge. Anker rates it at 25% on an iPhone 17 Pro in 10 minutes, then to 50% in 25 minutes, which is the kind of speed you’d normally expect from a wired charging session.

The MagGo 2 Pro battery is 10,000mAh, which is enough for a little over one full charge of an iPhone Pro Max and closer to two on a standard iPhone. Size-wise, it has about the same footprint as the iPhone itself and is roughly an ounce lighter than Anker’s standard MagGo. It’s not a slim battery, but for one with a fan, it’s workable in your travel bag, crossbody, etc.

Industry observers note that the single USB-C port works both directions at up to 45 watts. If you plug in a 45-watt charger to it, the MagGo 2 Pro can charge from empty to 80% in under an hour. The same port will charge a Mac or an iPad up to 45 watts in a pinch, which is a nice add-on for a MagSafe battery. You are not going to charge up your MacBook Pro from zero to full with it, but it’s a nice way to get a little charge in an emergency at the airport, etc.

According to recent reports, one thing to know before you buy: the cable in the box is a 1-foot USB-C-to-USB-C cable, and Anker states that reaching the full 45-watt recharge speed requires a 45-watt-rated cable. So keep that in mind as you pack for a trip.

Anker put a small display on the side that cycles through six screens with a side button: charging wattage, battery percentage, battery health, and temperature. It’s a nice touch to know you are reaching the 25-watt Qi 2.2 speed.

Recent findings suggest that there’s also a built-in stand that adjusts from flat to 80 degrees and folds back into the body when you’re done. You can also promptly turn off charging if you simply want to use it as a stand. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro comes in Phantom Gray, Burgundy Red, Polar Night Blue, and Starlight Silver.

It has been revealed that qi2.2 is the Holy Grail of MagSafe chargers, but as I said in the beginning, it’s irrelevant if the heat throttles it. To get full 25-watt MagSafe charging on the go, you’ll likely need something with a fan, unless you’re in colder weather. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro solves that problem with a built-in fan, a handy side display, and a stand.

The Anker MagGo 2 Pro is available on Amazon and directly from Anker.

Recent findings suggest that british-American brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate are currently awaiting extradition to the U.K., where they face dozens of charges including rape and trafficking for the purpose of sexual exploitation. The photos they posted on social media as they rose to fame — of men in tight pants, gripping thick cigars in their teeth, leaning against luxury sports cars next to massive-breasted women in bikinis — helped to establish the manosphere, and have become tropes in their own right. Their exploits — running a cam-girl empire out of Romania, which allegedly engaged in human trafficking — have been widely documented, as have their denials that they engaged in any kind of illegal activity.

But how did they really make that money, and who are the survivors they’ve left in their wake? The fresh documentary, Andrew Tate: Toxic Empire, attempts to answer those questions, using interviews with former members of their exclusive networking group, the War Room; with women who allege they were sexually assaulted by the brothers, including the former anti-feminist provocateur Lauren Southern; and those who knew them in their younger days, including Andrew’s fellow Big Brother castmember, who was there during his brief run on the British reality show back in 2016. (Like everything else, the brothers deny the allegations of sexual assault.).

Though many have tried to make sense of their story, Toxic Empire lays it out in stark relief: their childhood in the council flats of Luton, England, far away from their chess-master father back in the states; their short-lived stints as kickboxers; their entry into the cam-girl management business, long before OnlyFans made online sex work mainstream; and their brotherly dynamic, with Andrew, 39, taking the front seat, while his younger brother, 38, played support.

The first two parts of the four-part docuseries premieres on Nov. 25 at 9 p.m. on ID; the next two episodes will come out over the following two weeks, and all of them will be available on HBO Max after they air. Here’s three things we learned from the first two episodes. These are the days when anything goes.

According to recent reports, the holiday shopping season is here, and Apple Watch is always a popular gift. Apple’s lineup includes the affordable Apple Watch SE 3 and the more advanced Apple Watch Series 12.

Here’s how those two Apple Watch models stack up….

The Apple Watch SE 3 is the most affordable way to enter the Apple Watch ecosystem. It got a significant revision last year, adding a variety of new higher-end Apple Watch features. It now offers an Always-On display, sleep apnea notifications, temperature sensing, interactive wrist flick and double tap gestures, and more.

The Apple Watch SE 3 offers 18 hours of battery life, though you can stretch that to 32 hours in Low Power Mode. It supports fast charging, going from 0-80% in 45 minutes.

In a recent development, even though it hasn’t been updated in a year, the Apple Watch SE 3 is a very compelling option, especially for people new to the Apple Watch ecosystem. It’s pretty fantastic that you can get an Apple Watch with key display and health-monitoring features for under $200.

The Apple Watch Series 12 is Apple’s newest smartwatch, and it’s a substantial update over its predecessor. This year, Apple doubled down on the health and fitness capabilities of Apple Watch with an all-upcoming Health Sensing System.

Apple touts that the Apple Watch Series 12 delivers “the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” In fact, the company conducted a study of more than 1,000 participants that found the Series 12 “achieved statistically better overall accuracy than every competing wearable it tested across workouts and daily activities.”.

With the upcoming system, Apple Watch Series 12 captures your heart rate every five seconds. Previous Apple Watch models, including the Apple Watch SE 3, take measurements every five minutes. The new Health Sensing System also enables a new readiness score feature, which factors in your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score.

Recent findings suggest that as I wrote in my review, the Apple Watch Series 12 brings some of the biggest improvements to Apple Watch health tracking in years. The newly introduced sensing system unlocks a trove of new data along with better accuracy.

It has been revealed that the Apple Watch lineup is incredibly strong right now. Whether you’re deciding between the SE 3 and Series 12, both offer great health tracking, battery life, and connectivity. The Apple Watch SE 3 is an excellent choice for people newly introduced to the Apple Watch ecosystem.

The Apple Watch Series 12, however, is the best Apple Watch for most people. There are major improvements to the health tracking capabilities, offering meaningful steps forward in what the Apple Watch can tell you about yourself. In the two months I’ve had mine, I’ve come to appreciate the more frequent heart rate measurement and readiness score.

Industry News: How did pinwheel calculators work?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Coredump

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that as a handful of readers might know, I am a bit of a calculator nerd.
  • A video is worth a thousand tokens, so to explore the ingenuity of the design, let’s start with a short clip of a Vaucanson calculator from my collection:.
  • In a recent development, in the first half of the video, I demonstrate addition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that as a handful of readers might know, I am a bit of a calculator nerd. I’m especially fond of mechanical four-function calculators that had their heyday between the 1920s and 1960s and then disappeared without a trace.

A video is worth a thousand tokens, so to explore the ingenuity of the design, let’s start with a short clip of a Vaucanson calculator from my collection:.

In a recent development, in the first half of the video, I demonstrate addition. I calculate 1234 + 4321 by placing the first operand in the input register, turning the crank clockwise to add this value to the accumulator (bottom right), and then entering the second operand and cranking again. To subtract from the stored value, I’d turn the crank counterclockwise.

Recent findings suggest that the second and more interesting half shows multiplication: I solve 79 × 123 by entering the first operand and then turning the crank three times to load 79 × 3 into the accumulator. Next, I shift the accumulator carriage one decimal digit to the right and crank twice; because the accumulator is offset from the input register, this has the same effect as cranking twenty times in the original position; in other words, I add 79 × 20. Finally, I shift the carriage once more and complete one more turn to add 79 × 100. Note that the crank counter in the bottom left now reads “123”, confirming that we multiplied the first operand by the correct value.

To divide, I’d load the first operand into the accumulator and then successively subtract power-of-ten multiples of the second number. This would give me the integer result in the counter register and the remainder in the accumulator.

According to recent reports, alright — so how does this work? Well, if you pop open a pinwheel calculator, you will be greeted by a pretty complicated mechanism:.

Industry observers note that there’s a lot going on here, but the most important part of the assembly is the prominent stack of input disks, one per digit, as seen in the top right of the photo. Each disk has three main components: a center section mounted to a keyed shaft that stays in position until the main crank is turned; a set of nine radial pins that slide into grooves machined in that disk; and a freely-moving digit-setting ring with a track and a couple of detents:.

It has been revealed that each pin has a protrusion that rides in the track of the digit-setting ring. By turning the input lever, we can change the number of pins that extend from the assembly.

When the crank is turned, these extended pins mesh to an intermediate gear that advances the digit at the corresponding position of the accumulator:.

It has been revealed that of course, this mechanism is not enough: without a way to carry to the next column, 0001 + 0009 would give us 0000 instead of 0010. To implement carry, each input disk (except for the rightmost one) is also equipped with a spring-loaded carry pin. This pin sticks out at all times, but is normally out of the path of the intermediate gear, so it has no effect on the output value.

In a recent development, to perform carry, each output position is equipped with a cam that pushes a wedge-shaped carry-sensing lever into the path of the carry pin just as the digit rolls over from 9 to 0. This wedge pushes the pin to the left, momentarily placing it in the path of the intermediate gear for the next decimal digit.

This is a mouthful; the entire process is shown in the following video:.

The carry-sensing lever is pushed back into the retracted position before the drum completes a full rotation, thus allowing the carry pin to spring back.

Note that the carry pins are staggered and do not engage at all once; this is to allow carry to effortlessly ripple through all digits if necessary (e.g., when adding 9999 + 1).

Sources indicate that there’s a couple of additional convenience and reliability features in each pinwheel calculator; this includes interlocks to prevent out-of-sequence inputs, as well as reset levers for each register. There’s even a mechanical bell on overflow or underflow. I won’t bore you with all the gory details, in part because these mechanisms are less interesting — but if you’re morbidly curious, this ancient YouTube video provides a more complete walkthrough.

And if you want to learn about the prehistory of calculators, I invite you to check out my 2023 article:.

According to recent reports, PS. Yep, this is why one of the registers on all Intel CPUs is called the “accumulator”.

Pressure relief score (out of 5).

It has been revealed that temperature regulation: Reliable temperature regulation is an notable feature of a mattress for back pain. Waking up hot and sweaty can lead to more movement (like kicking off the covers), which can cause further injury. Pressure relief: This is a term to describe how much cushioning there is along the touch points of the mattress. For example, for side sleepers, this will be your shoulders, hips and knees. For back sleepers, this will likely be your lumbar region and upper back and shoulders. Minimal pressure relief can lead to a build-up of pressure, which can exacerbate existing pain. Edge Support: This describes how sturdy a mattress is at its edges and corners. This is an important feature for any mattress, but especially those with back pain who may need to sit comfortably and safely before standing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this week, Silver Bullet Band bassist Chris Campbell, who played alongside Bob Seger from 1969 through his final tour in 2019, died of natural causes at 78. Tributes poured in from across the music world, and now Seger himself has weighed in.

“With the passing of our bassist and my friend for over 55 years, Chris Campbell, it’s taken me a couple of days to put my thoughts together, such a huge and sad loss,” Seger wrote in a statement. “Chris was with us as we started out traveling to gigs in station wagons and vans and for the next forty plus years - all the way through our last show in 2019.

It has been revealed that “He was a great musician,” Seger continued. “Chris understood well the roots of rock and roll, rhythm and blues. His ability to lock into a pocket with a drummer was extraordinary and he was remarkably consistent show to show. Off stage, his sense of humor kept us laughing and entertained. Chris was like family; we raised our kids together. It was a blessing to share this journey with Chris, and I’ll cherish the memories forever. RIP my friend.”.

Campbell joined the Bob Seger System in 1969, just one year after “Ramblin’ Gamblin’ Man” became their first nationwide hit. “I was hired in what I thought was a temporary job as bass player because Dan Honaker had just broken his wrist about a week before the Mongrel tour [in a motorcycle accident],” Campbell told Rolling Stone in 2011. “I had a week to prepare. I had to learn this album frontwards and backwards.”.

It has been revealed that the Bob Seger System dissolved a few years later, but Seger kept Campbell in mind when he formed a new group not long afterwards. “He remarked, ‘I’m thinking of putting a band together,'” Campbell told Rolling Stone. “I said to him, ‘That’s kind of bizarre, I have a keyboard player and a drummer.’ He goes, ‘I got a guitarist, Drew Abbott.’ That was the start of the Silver Bullet Band.”.

Anthropic is launching a new tool for builders called Claude Ship. The new AI feature allows Claude to “review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows.”.

Recent findings suggest that claude Ship is a latest product created especially for builders who code with agents. The idea is to make handling pull requests as automated as agentic coding.

“That’s why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta,” Anthropic says. “It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what’s ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person. The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.”.

Claude Ship is comprised of three agents: Code Review, PR Steward, and Claude Approvals.

“Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually,” Anthropic indicates.

“Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the fresh /ship command in Claude Code,” Anthropic says.

More importantly, if you already own the HW-Q990F or even the older HW-Q990D, upgrading probably will not feel dramatic enough to justify the cost. But for someone starting from TV speakers or an entry-level soundbar, this system can completely change how movies, games, and even sports feel at home.

Sources indicate that andy Taylor, the founding guitarist in Duran Duran who co-wrote several of the group’s most beloved songs, including “Hungry Like The Wolf,” “Rio,” and “Girls on Film,” died Monday after a long battle with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer. He was 65.

Taylor’s death was confirmed Wednesday with a statement from Duran Duran and Taylor’s family.

“Andy was there at the very beginning of our story,” Duran Duran said. “From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.”.

In a recent development, the band noted Taylor faced his cancer battle with “remarkable courage, honesty and grace,” adding, “It was great to make music with him again when the original five reunited in the early 2000s, and that time together, both on stage and in the studio, meant a tremendous amount to all of us. When we were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022, Andy was too unwell to join us, but his words that night reminded everyone of his strength and the bond we shared.”.

Taylor’s wife, Tracey, mentioned, “”To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather. He was the rock of our family. For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home.

Recent findings suggest that “Andy faced the last few years with so much courage and determination. He never gave up, fighting until the very end, never losing his love of life. The kindness and support shown to him by fans from all over the world throughout his illness brought him immense comfort and strength, and for that we will always be grateful.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

Because they were still playing FM rock in America; we were the only New Wave band that had heavy guitar, so it crossed over.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Literally from the day I met Nick, John, Simon and Roger they truly valued the contribution of a rather noisy, versatile Northern brat,” Andy Taylor noted in 2022. “We all grew up on the same vinyl records and live gigs, from David Bowie to Roxy Music, the Sex Pistols and of course Chic. I could go to all those places as a player and developed a hybrid guitar style that fitted this amazing concept for a band.”.

In 1984, Taylor formed Power Station with Robert Palmer, Chic drummer Tony Thompson, and Duran Duran bassist John Taylor. Sources indicate that taylor grew up in the Northeast England town of Cullercoats. He learned guitar as a teenager and played around England in a series of unsuccessful groups until 1980 when he came across an ad in Melody Maker by a latest band in Birmingham seeking a “Live Wire Guitarist.”When he arrived in Birmingham for the audition, he met Rhodes along with bassist John Taylor and drummer Roger Taylor. “The three of us had a good laugh about the fact that by coincidence we all shared the same surname,” Andy Taylor wrote in his 2008 memoir Wild Boy. “They had long, floppy hair and were into David Bowie and Bryan Ferry and the whole new fashion trend that had started to gain currency ever since punk died away.”.

Recent findings suggest that this was the start of the Fresh Romantic scene, and Duran Duran would become its most famous export once they teamed up with frontman Simon Le Bon. The band’s 1981 debut single “Planet Earth” became an immediate hit in England and set the tone for much of the music that followed by mixing New Wave synthesizers with Andy Taylor’s searing electric guitar.

Industry observers note that by the time they released their second LP, 1982’s Rio, MTV had launched in America. The fledgling cable channel, desperate for content, put the videos for singles “Hungry Like the Wolf” and “Rio” into heavy rotation and turned the band into superstars. The group became so popular that the press labeled them the leaders of a “Second British Invasion” alongside groups like Spandau Ballet, Flock of Seagulls, Human League, Dexy’s Midnight Runners, and Eurythmics.The hits continued in 1983 when the band released Seven and the Ragged Tiger, featuring the “Union of the Snake” and “The Reflex,” but the group was melting down behind the scenes due to personality clashes, disagreements over the band’s musical direction, and heavy cocaine use.

In a recent development, in 1984, during a break in the Duran Duran schedule, Andy Taylor and John Taylor formed Power Station with Palmer. “The music that John and I made together in Power station was born partly out of frustration at not being able to play the way we wanted in Duran Duran,” Taylor wrote in Wild Boy. “The memory of how painstaking it had been to record Seven and the Ragged Tiger was still fresh in our minds, so when the opportunity came along to do something different we seized it with both hands.

Industry observers note that the warring factions of Duran Duran were forced back together in 1985 to perform at Live Aid in Philadelphia. “We’d reached rock bottom and we had absolutely nothing to say to each other,” Taylor wrote in Wild Boy. “We drove to the venue through streets packed with excited rock fans, but inside the bus the atmosphere was as if we were on a way to a funeral. Little did we realize that we were on the way to a funeral – it was ours.”.

Sources indicate that andy Taylor quit Duran Duran the following year to start a solo career that stalled after two unsuccessful albums: 1987’s Thunder and 1990’s Dangerous. He spent much of the Nineties spending time with his wife Tracy and their children Andy, Georgie, Bethy, and Izzy.

Industry observers note that duran Duran scored a massive comeback in 1993 thanks to the hits “Ordinary World” and “Come Undone,” but were on a downward spiral at the turn of the millennium with only Simon Le Bon and Nick Rhodes remaining from the original band. They reunited with the classic lineup — Andy Taylor included — for a reunion tour in 2001 that led to the 2004 LP Astronaut. Ticket sales were strong, but old problems quickly resurfaced. Andy Taylor left the band during the making of an album in 2006 following months of tension with the group and their management.

Sources indicate that taylor kept a low profile in the decade following his departure from Duran Duran. The iconic YouTube app icon that looked like a retro TV found on iOS might be making a comeback, with new customizable icons showing up behind the scenes of a new YouTube patch.

In the early days of the iPhone, Apple built a custom app for YouTube on iOS before Google built its own. That included an app icon that looked like a retro TV and it was later replaced when YouTube’s official app released on the platform.

Now, that icon might be coming back.

Android Authority spotted several upcoming app icons YouTube for Android is testing in its latest beta update (v21.47.483-BETA). These icons seem to be tied to a new feature that would allow users to customize the homescreen icon for YouTube, and includes seven designs in total including two throwback designs. One is the aforementioned retro TV icon used on iOS, which was never on YouTube for Android, and another is an old stacked YouTube logo design.

That noted, it’s very fun to get these throwbacks, and we’ll be excited to see this functionality go live.

The Ring Indoor Cam 2K is 58% off at $24.99 (originally $59.99), while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is 60% off at $39.99 (originally $99.99)—both at their lowest-ever price.

Industry observers note that it also has a removable lens cover to block the camera’s view, which is a nice privacy perk, though closing the cover doesn’t turn off the microphone. For complete audio privacy, you need to disable the microphone in the Ring app.

It has a 140-degree horizontal and vertical field of view that provides head-to-toe framing, plus up to 6x zoom for better detail. You can install it without wiring, though you’ll need to recharge its built-in battery. It also requires a 2.4GHz wifi network.

The main catch with both devices is the ongoing subscription cost: Live viewing, two-way talk, and basic real-time notifications all work without a subscription, but reviewing saved footage requires a paid initiative, starting at $4.99 per month or $49.99 annually for one device; coverage for multiple devices at one location starts at $9.99 monthly or $99.99 annually.

Sources indicate that at these prices, the Ring Indoor Cam 2K is perfect for occasional live check-ins, while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is better suited to monitoring your front entrance. Buying both makes sense if you already have a Ring proposal that covers extra devices.

OpenAI is bringing GPT-6.2 Sol to the Chat tab in ChatGPT today, less than a week after the model debuted in Work and Codex. The company also set a retirement date for two older models.

It has been revealed that openAI states it tuned this version of Sol for everyday conversation. It’s better at picking out details in photos, like the symbols on a parking sign, and following your instructions when searching the web.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re comparing hotels for a weekend trip, for example, ChatGPT can weigh a shorter walk against a lower nightly rate. It can also offer to alert you when something you’re shopping for drops in price.

The global rollout starts today for ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise customers.

As for the outgoing models, OpenAI says it will retire GPT-5.6 Sol from Chat, Work, and Codex on December 23.

GPT-5.6 Terra will also leave ChatGPT Work and Codex on the same day next month.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the 75-inch Hisense U6SF Pro has dropped to $747.97 from $1,399.99 for Black Friday sale—bringing it to its lowest price to date.
  • For a budget set, the U6 Pro gets a lot right when it comes to picture quality—its high peak brightness helps it hold up during a sunny afternoon in a living room with big windows, so a daytime football game or cooking show won’t look washed out, while its excellent contrast and effective local dimming keep dark scenes looking deep when you settle in for a movie at night.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the 75-inch Hisense U6SF Pro has dropped to $747.97 from $1,399.99 for Black Friday sale—bringing it to its lowest price to date. The rest of the U6 Pro lineup is discounted as well, so you can pick up the same TV in sizes from 55 inches to a massive 100 inches, for anyone with the room for something closer to a home-theater-sized screen. Whichever size you choose, you’ll get free delivery to the room of choice—a service that normally costs $19.99. As for the TV itself, it’s a 2026 model that sits below the U7SG (also on sale for $1,297.99, from $1,999.99) in Hisense's lineup as the brand's entry point into Mini LED, pairing a 4K panel and local dimming with a matte, anti-reflective coating meant to cut down on glare, notes this PCMag review.

For a budget set, the U6 Pro gets a lot right when it comes to picture quality—its high peak brightness helps it hold up during a sunny afternoon in a living room with big windows, so a daytime football game or cooking show won’t look washed out, while its excellent contrast and effective local dimming keep dark scenes looking deep when you settle in for a movie at night. It also does a good job cleaning up lower-quality content, which is useful for older cable broadcasts or compressed YouTube videos—and its Fire TV interface makes it easy to jump between those kinds of content and the major streaming services without needing a separate streaming device.

Sources indicate that the U6 Pro also brings plenty to the table for gaming, with HDMI 2.1, VRR, ALLM, and a 144Hz refresh rate that PC gamers can push to 240Hz at a lower 1080p resolution. That stated, the panel’s slow response time and poor motion performance can reportedly make fast-moving scenes look noticeably blurry. Viewing angles are limited too, with the picture losing quality fairly rapidly when you move off-center—and its built-in speakers aren’t particularly impressive either, so a soundbar could be worth budgeting for.

One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated.

A novel solution for connecting to the internet on the go, the TP-Link Roam 7 travel router is now down to $83.49 from $119.99 for Black Friday, marking its lowest price to date. This isn't a full-size home router but, as the name suggests, a compact travel companion that measures roughly the size of a paperback book, with foldable antennas that let it slip easily into a bag.

More about convenience than chasing top speeds, you can use the Roam 7 as a standard router, connect it to public wifi to create a private network, or share your phone's internet through USB tethering. It also supports Ethernet input and USB modems, along with range extender and wireless client modes. That flexibility is particularly useful when you’re juggling a laptop, phone, and maybe a tablet and would prefer not to sign each one into a shaky network separately. Setup is straightforward through the TP-Link Tether app: scan a QR code, choose your connection type, and you’re online in a few minutes.

In a recent development, once it’s running, the hardware covers the basics, with a 2.5 Gbps port for a wired connection like a hotel’s Ethernet jack, a 1 Gbps port for a wired device, and a USB 3.0 port for a storage drive or phone tethering. And since it draws power over USB-C (5V/3A), a basic power bank can keep it going through a long layover or a camping trip. As handy as it is on the road, though, it’s not meant to replace a full-size home router—even with its 5 GHz band and Wi-Fi 7 support—which will generally offer better coverage and more consistent speeds. Real-world performance also depends heavily on your connection and setup. USB tethering, for example, can feel slower than using your phone directly. It also leaves out features like automatic band steering, so you may end up managing networks yourself. Still, if you travel often or need a portable network hub for multiple devices, you’ll find it holds up pretty well.

#108449. Smart people who give a shit use tools

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1843 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Iankduncan ↗ Open Full Page

Smart people who give a shit use tools

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1843 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Iankduncan

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, anyone who has worked on payment rails or old distributed systems knows the exact feeling Justin Michael describes in his post this week.
  • Halfway down the page, though, the essay takes a turn I’ve been seeing a lot lately, and it bugs me.
  • The implication is pretty hard to miss: if you’re using AI, you’re giving up on giving a shit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, anyone who has worked on payment rails or old distributed systems knows the exact feeling Justin Michael describes in his post this week. You peel back the curtain on some piece of infrastructure the economy quietly runs on, expecting Swiss watchmaking, and find duct tape, twenty-year-old batch files, and three people in the whole tech giant who know why you never reboot box four on a Tuesday. He calls them “smart people who give a shit,” and he’s dead right that they are the main reason the lights stay on.

Halfway down the page, though, the essay takes a turn I’ve been seeing a lot lately, and it bugs me. Michael points to the recent run of massive outages (Microsoft 365, United, major banks, Apple) and blames leadership for trying to swap those people out for generative AI. Fair enough; there’s probably plenty of truth in that. But he doesn’t stop at bad management. By the end, the tools themselves have become the acid dissolving whoever picks them up. “Every prompt moves them one step further away from the system they used to know inside and out,” he writes. Every generated line robs engineers of the struggle that makes them smart and the ownership that makes them care.

The implication is pretty hard to miss: if you’re using AI, you’re giving up on giving a shit.

In a recent development, I use these tools every day on systems where bugs cost significant sums of money or wedge production queues, and my experience has been almost the exact opposite. More than anything else, LLMs amplify who you already are. Deeply curious, caring people can dramatically amplify what they produce and how thoroughly they understand it. Lazy bums can, for now, coast as meat proxies for a chat window, ferrying tickets into a prompt box and clicking merge on whatever falls out.

Recent findings suggest that think about what “giving a shit” actually meant on a normal engineering team before 2024. Mostly, it meant fighting a losing war against the clock. You’d spot a nasty race condition in a state machine and know you should model it in TLA+, or write a property test that hammers every interleaving, or go read the forty-thousand-line service downstream to be certain your assumption held. Half the time you didn’t, because doing it properly took two days you didn’t have and three other fires were waiting. So you eyeballed the diff, wrote a unit test for the happy path, left a slightly nervous comment, and hoped nobody touched that file for a while. Caring was rarely limited by how much people wanted to do the right thing. It was rationed by how fast one human could read and type.

In a recent development, when you hand a capable model to that engineer, they don’t suddenly shrug and rubber-stamp the first draft. They finally write the TLA+ spec. They pull on the threads they were always curious about, digging into why a gnarly legacy subsystem behaves the way it does instead of treating it as a black box. They build a real simulator for the flaky third-party API nobody ever had time to mock properly. They have the model trace every caller of a legacy function across a sprawling monorepo before changing its contract, instead of grepping for five minutes and praying. They write the exhaustive edge-case tests and run mutation testing against the parts that keep them awake at night.

The kind of rigor that used to be reserved for people writing avionics software or working at Bell Labs is suddenly cheap enough to pull off on an ordinary Thursday. Calling that “caring less” has the whole thing backwards.

Then there is the other side of the amplifier. Anyone who has reviewed a 1,500-line pull request written by a meat proxy who clearly hit “accept all,” got a green linter, and blanked out when asked to explain line 400 knows exactly what Michael is furious about. (I’m certainly guilty of opening massive AI-assisted PRs myself, though in the service of giving a shit, so the line count by itself isn’t the crime.) Prompt, paste, and pray is very real, and it produces miserable software. I’ve written before about the specific sinking feeling of staring at 800 lines of generated code you have no mental model of and deploying it with crossed fingers.

There’s a subtler hazard too, especially for people early in their careers: if you never wrestle with a weird bug or read a stack trace yourself, you never build the scar tissue that tells you when something smells wrong. And LLMs make laziness unusually tempting because of how they fail. A compiler yells at you loudly when you screw up; a model fails in smooth, confident prose that looks totally reasonable until production catches fire. That’s a genuine risk, and pretending it isn’t would be silly.

Still, look closely at what’s actually broken in that scenario. The trouble comes from shipping code nobody verified, without building a mental model, in an organization where nobody feels on the hook when it breaks. We had that exact engineer long before ChatGPT demonstrated up. Ten years ago they pasted the top Stack Overflow answer without reading the comments, pulled in a bloated dependency to avoid thinking for twenty minutes, and stamped “LGTM” on every review after thirty seconds. Now they can coast as a human clipboard for a model, at least for a while, until the production bugs pile up or someone realizes a cron job could do the clipboard part cheaper. Take away their LLM tomorrow and they won’t suddenly start caring about ACH edge cases. They’ll just go back to shipping carelessness at a slower clip.

Look at Michael’s own example of ACH. The people keeping banking rails alive aren’t chiseling NACHA files into stone tablets to stay spiritually close to the metal. Their care shows up in reconciliation scripts, monitors, static checks, runbooks, and custom tooling they built because unaided human attention breaks down on systems this messy. Every jump up the abstraction ladder (compilers, garbage collectors, search engines, high-level frameworks) brought the exact same warning that we were moving another step away from the machine and losing the people who really understood it. Sure, far fewer programmers today can hand-assemble x86 than in 1985. Meanwhile, the systems we have to keep upright grew by several orders of magnitude. Without stronger leverage, you don’t get a golden age of artisanal engineering where everyone holds the whole codebase in their head. You just get more critical systems that nobody understands at all, because they long ago outgrew what one unaided brain can hold.

There is a bigger elephant in the room about all those outages, too, and it predates LLMs by a long shot. A huge share of the instability we are watching right now is the bill coming due for forty years of insufficient engineering rigor. Giving a shit does not make people infallible. Some of the smartest, most conscientious engineers in the industry spent decades building critical infrastructure in memory-unsafe languages, gluing together under-specified protocols, skipping formal verification, and shipping state machines whose edge cases lived only inside one person’s head. Heroics and tribal knowledge kept the wheels on, right up until they didn’t.

Sources indicate that plenty of the vulnerabilities and failure modes knocking systems over today have been sitting quietly in the wild for years, or even decades. We got away with them because nobody had the time or budget to poke every dark corner of a sprawling legacy stack, and because change moved slowly enough for manual patching to keep up. Only now is the matter being forced, by automated bug-hunting that never sleeps, by decades of accumulated coupling, and by systems that have finally grown too tangled for human heroics to paper over. Blaming all of that on AI slop is a comforting story, because it implies we can just go back to the old way of working and everything will steady out. The old way of working is how we ended up with a world where bad updates and long-dormant bugs can wobble major banks, airlines, and cloud providers in the same week.

None of that lets leadership off the hook. Where Michael is completely on target is what’s happening in the executive suite. Leadership looking at an LLM and thinking, fantastic, now we can lay off the prickly senior engineers who push back on bad ideas and replace them with a $200-a-month subscription, really is a slow-motion train wreck, and it makes a fragile landscape much worse. To someone who has never been paged at three in the morning, a fragile system held aloft by quiet competence and a pile of plausible-looking slop look identical on a quarterly slide deck.

According to recent reports, that disease, though, is decades older than generative AI. It’s the exact same management fantasy that gave us “let’s fire the expensive in-house team and outsource the core platform to the lowest bidder,” “let’s cut QA because developers can test their own stuff,” and “let’s lay off twenty percent of engineering while keeping the roadmap unchanged.” AI didn’t invent the belief that engineers are interchangeable output factories. It just handed executives a shinier, cheaper-sounding excuse to run the same playbook again.

That’s why lumping AI-using engineers in with the executives hollowing out their companies does real harm. Telling the story as “AI makes engineers dumb and indifferent” accidentally writes bad leadership an alibi: shucks, the fresh technology didn’t live up to the hype, who could have known? And on the way there, it sneers at the people in the trenches who are grabbing every piece of leverage they can find to keep increasingly absurd systems from falling over.

It has been revealed that if you want to know whether someone gives a shit about a system, asking whether they used an LLM is the wrong question. Ask what happens when the code they merged breaks at two in the morning. Ask whether “the model wrote it” flies as an excuse in code review. Ask whether they have the time, standing, and backing to tell a VP that a deadline is reckless.

Companies lose smart people who give a shit when they strip away ownership, punish dissent, and reward shipping volume over reliability. Give those same people real stakes and a good model, and they don’t check out. They finally get to build the guardrails, proofs, and fixes they never had the hours to build before.

Michael is right that capitalism has its hand squarely on a hot stove right now, and that the rest of us are getting burned while executives relearn that you can’t automate away accountability. I just wish we’d aim the anger at the people making that bet, instead of pretending that giving a shit requires typing every character by hand.

Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones are 45% off right now, down to $199 for Black Friday, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet. Colors include in Dewdrop Mint, Eucalyptus Green, and Hazelnut Taupe. Weighing around 8.1 ounces, they’re among the lightest premium noise-canceling headphones, with generously padded earcups and a cushioned headband that spreads pressure without gripping too tightly, making them comfortable to wear for extended periods. They’re also easy to pack for travel, as the earcups fold and swivel for storage in the included hard-shell carrying case. The removable earpads are another welcome touch, since you can replace them as they wear down without having to retire the entire pair.

Comfort aside, noise cancellation is another area where these headphones deliver, doing a particularly good job of reducing lower-frequency rumble and background chatter, though some higher-pitched voices can still come through, notes this PCMag review. As for their sound profile, it leans warm and bass-forward, with deep lows that suit bass-heavy genres, while the companion app adds Bose Immersive Audio for spatial sound and lets you create customized listening profiles—the three-band EQ is fairly basic, though, so anyone who likes fine-tuning their sound may find the adjustment options limiting.

It has been revealed that connectivity, too, brings some useful upgrades over the previous generation, including Bluetooth 5.4, multipoint pairing for two devices, Google Fast Pair, and lossless audio over USB-C. That same USB-C port lets you charge the headphones while you listen, and the included USB-C-to-3.5mm cable covers standard headphone jacks, including the ones on in-flight entertainment systems. That stated, battery life is less impressive, topping out at 24 hours with ANC enabled, although a 15-minute charge adds around 2.5 hours of playback. Wireless audio is also limited to the standard AAC and SBC codecs, with no support for the higher-quality aptX Adaptive—a feature available on Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra Headphones.

While tech can get pretty expensive, especially in our current "RAMageddon" era, there are still plenty of affordable devices out there. The problem, of course, isn't quantity, but quality: Buying a tech item for under $50 is risky, since many of these products are made as cheaply as possible. If you're looking for a portable Bluetooth speaker, for instance, you don't want to buy something with poor sound quality, or that doesn't easily connect to your devices, or that breaks unexpectedly.

You don't need to worry about any of that with the JBL Go 4. This is a solid portable speaker that just so happens to have an MSRP of $49.95. It's so good, I named it Lifehacker's best gift under $50, as its price, excellent sound quality, and feature set make it a great option for most anyone on your list. It's an even better buy during Black Friday, too: Right now, you can pick up the JBL Go 4 for as low as $31.95, 36% off the original retail price.

Recent findings suggest that JBL's Go 4 is a small speaker, but it gets surprisingly loud—especially for a speaker at this price point. Like other JBL speakers, it places a particular emphasis on bass. This is a tiny speaker, so don't expect a subwoofer on the go, but not only will it let you hear the bass in your music, it is noticeably punchy. JBL advertises seven hours of playtime on a single charge here, which is often plenty for taking the speaker out and about for the day. You can net an additional two hours of if you engage "Playtime Boost." JBL doesn't specify how this works, but it likely cuts some of the frequencies here to save on battery life. And, since it's 1P67-rated against dust and water, it's a great choice for outdoor use.

Perhaps my favorite thing about the JBL Go 4 is that it supports Auracast. That means you can easily connect to any other Auracast-compatible JBL speaker using the Auracast button on each device. I've used this before at parties and gatherings for an impromptu multi-speaker setup. Since JBL is so popular, it's not impractical to assume one or two other people at the function might have a similar speaker you can connect to, or if you know friends or family members have JBL speakers of their own, you can coordinate these setups ahead of time.

This discount is only available on specific colors of the Go 4, at least on Amazon: Black, White, Blue, Purple, Red, and "Squad." Black and Orange, Pink, and Sand are all still $49.95. Again, the JBL Go 4 is absolutely worth the $50 MSRP, but unless you're married to one of those three colors, it's even better at a discount.

According to recent reports, in short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Industry observers note that the best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

But as I always say to my fellow friends and family, just because a show is trending doesn’t necessarily mean it’s worth your time.

That’s why I’ve been digging through this week’s most-watched picks to find the ones that genuinely deserve a spot on your watchlist. I’ve narrowed things down to three shows I’d happily recommend to anyone, including an epic fantasy adventure reaching its season finale, a compelling sports drama charting the early life of one of the greatest boxers of all time, and a romantic drama packed with some awkward relationship complications.

Recent findings suggest that this list is based on the Prime Video U.S. top 10 shows as of Wednesday, November 25, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” is wrapping up its eight-episode third season, with the final two episodes now available to stream. There’s even better news for fans, as Prime Video renewed the series for season 4 ahead of the finale, so there’s more Middle-earth to look forward to. The show has certainly made headlines for its enormous budget and ambitious production, with Amazon originally committing to a five-season initiative and involving the Tolkien Estate in overseeing the adaptation. It’s a fascinating chapter in the franchise’s television history, and thankfully, the story isn’t over yet.

According to recent reports, set five years after the fall of Eregion, the third season finds Middle-earth engulfed in war as Sauron’s (Charlie Vickers) armies continue their march across the land. With the Dark Lord establishing his stronghold in Mordor, he sets his sights on forging the One Ring, a powerful weapon that could secure his control over Middle-earth. Meanwhile, Galadriel (Morfydd Clark), Elrond (Robert Aramayo), Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) and their allies face mounting challenges as they attempt to unite the Elves, Dwarves and Men against him. As battles spread across the kingdoms, Sauron also works to enslave his ring-servants.

Watch "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" on Prime Video.

Industry observers note that “The Greatest” is still holding strong in Prime Video’s top 10, a biographical sports drama following four formative years in the life of Cassius Clay as he goes from promising amateur boxer to heavyweight champion Muhammad Ali. Rather than focusing entirely on his career in the ring, the series also explores the personal, family and cultural pressures that shaped him along the way. This is a more intimate approach to Ali’s story, while the faithful recreation of historic boxing footage also helps bring the story to life. It’s an interesting watch even if you’re not a huge boxing fan.

Based on the early life of legendary boxer Muhammad Ali (Jaalen Best), this eight-part drama follows his journey from Olympic gold medallist to heavyweight title contender. Formerly known as Cassius Clay, the young fighter returns to his hometown of Louisville after winning gold at the 1960 Rome Olympics, ready to take the next step in his boxing career. As he prepares for a career-defining showdown with formidable opponent Sonny Liston (Amin Joseph), the series charts the pivotal moments that helped shape one of boxing’s most recognizable figures.

Watch "The Greatest" on Prime Video.

Romance fans should give “Love in Disguise” a spot on their watchlist this week. Adapted from a web novel by Lee A-yeon and Ryu Do-ha, this Korean romantic comedy-thriller stars Yim Si-wan from Netflix’s “Squid Game” alongside Seorina. It’s also the first time the two actors have shared the screen, which gives the series an extra appeal for fans of both. The pair have spoken about wanting to capture the spirit of the original novel while giving the story their own spin. With romance, comedy and thriller elements in the mix, it’s an interesting option if you're after something a little different.

The series follows Kang Jae-hee (Seorina), a former special forces operative turned detective who takes on an unusual undercover assignment. Disguising herself as a man, she lands a job as the personal secretary to Yoon Yi-jun (Yim Si-wan), the wealthy heir to the Taekang Group, who is suspected of murdering his previous secretary. While keeping a close eye on her fresh employer and searching for evidence, Jae-hee finds herself caught up in the family’s complicated affairs. As Yi-jun begins to let his guard down, maintaining her cover becomes increasingly difficult, particularly as their relationship develops.

Watch "Love in Disguise" on Prime Video.

Sources indicate that jane Fonda, Robert De Niro and Chelsea Handler are among the entertainment figures who have signed on to a letter backing Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) in his bid to become Senate majority leader over Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-NY).

The letter, signed by about three dozen figures describing themselves as donors, fundraisers and artists, stated that in this year’s midterms, “voters delivered not on ly a mandate but an opportunity for change: a government that delivers real value in the daily lives of working families.”.

In a recent development, “That change will only come from renewed leadership with a vision for the future,” the letter stated. “The Democratic Party has a trust and credibility problem, and fixing it requires Senate leaders willing to challenge the entrenched interests and power structures that protect those in power, in both parties.” The letter also called on senators to support candidates “who are dedicated to accountability, transparency and the bold agenda voters demanded.” Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Al Gore To Purchase Hometown Paper Carthage Courier News MS NOW Hosts Sign On To Letter Urging Adoption Of "Fair" WGAE Contract; Network Says Talks Are Ongoing And "Constructive".

The election for majority leader, to be held early next month, has highlighted party divisions, including among donors and in the entertainment industry, and even after the whopping victories of Democrats across the country in the midterms.

Noting that the upcoming vote on a Senate leader will be chosen by secret ballot, the letter called on the caucus to support Van Hollen, who is challenging Schumer, the current minority leader who had been the presumptive favorite to win following Democrats huge gains in which they flipped control of the chamber.

Others who signed on to the letter include Bruce Cohen, Padma Lakshmi, Laurie David, David Mandel, Fisher Stevens, Marisa Tomei, Amy Ziering and Morgan Spector.

Sources indicate that in a statement. De Niro mentioned, “Americans voted for the change necessary to fight the corruption, cruelty, and policies of Trump and his Epstein class cronies. That’s why I’m supporting change in Senate leadership. Chris Van Hollen is a progressive leader and a fierce fighter. He’s the right person to lead the Senate majority.”.

Van Hollen has pitched his candidacy as a necessary response to the midterm results and that Democrats’ unexpected gains were also calls for change, coming from the left and the middle of the party.

“The voters responsible for the Blue Tsunami want fundamental change and bold, upcoming ideas. Simply put, Chuck Schumer is the past and Chris Van Hollen is the present and the future,” Cohen mentioned.

In a recent development, A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials. The database was neither password-protected nor encrypted.

The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” ….

Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler says that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.

It has been revealed that I also observed thousands of Tor .onion addresses associated with account names and passwords. The Tor .onion services are generally categorized as part of the dark web, and these credentials could potentially provide access to private forums, marketplaces, communication platforms, or other hidden services. While .onion accounts alone do not imply criminal or malicious activity, it is estimated that as much as 60% of dark web sites host illegal material and illicit activities. This is the first time I have seen a large number of dark web accounts in breached credentials. It should be noted that legitimate organizations, journalists, whistleblower platforms, and news organizations also operate .onion services to provide anonymity and bypass censorship.

But the most frightening aspect of it is separate folders for individual victims containing all of the information needed for identity theft.

Fowler told Wired that this data appears to have been obtained through advanced malware.

The “scariest” thing in the database, Fowler claims, was around 400,000 documents that appeared to come from “more advanced malware” compiling information about individual victims […] that create a detailed profile of an individual and their digital life. “If you had that, you own that person,” Fowler says.

There’s no information about the specific sources of the data, but it seems likely to be aggregated from a range of data breaches. Fowler contacted the hosting organization to have the database removed, but it’s not known how many people may have had access to it.

Sources indicate that the best protection is to use a password manager like Apple’s Passwords app to ensure you have strong, unique passwords for each individual website and service you use, with two-factor authentication enabled wherever possible. When given the choice of 2FA code delivery, you should always opt for an authenticator app rather than a text message to protect yourself against SIM-swap attacks.
