💡 Key Takeaways
  • Eight years ago, I bought my first Philips Hue product: the Hue Go Portable Lamp.
  • Philips Hue is one of the few tech ecosystems I’ve genuinely enjoyed investing in, and one that has become more valuable to me over time.
  • Ahead of the shopping holiday, I asked Marco Merolla, Executive Vice President and Business Leader of Connected Lighting at Philips Hue, about the company's approach to affordability, product longevity and the future of smart lighting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eight years ago, I bought my first Philips Hue product: the Hue Go Portable Lamp. Eight years later, the bowl-shaped, battery-powered lamp still works, and it has quite a few friends.

Philips Hue is one of the few tech ecosystems I’ve genuinely enjoyed investing in, and one that has become more valuable to me over time. But Philips Hue does have a reputation for being expensive. That's why I consider Black Friday deals one of the best opportunities to either get started with Hue or expand an existing setup.

Ahead of the shopping holiday, I asked Marco Merolla, Executive Vice President and Business Leader of Connected Lighting at Philips Hue, about the company's approach to affordability, product longevity and the future of smart lighting.

His answers shed some light on why customers like me keep coming back, and where there's still room for improvement when it comes to connected smart homes.

It has been revealed that I'm vehemently anti-major-light. One of my proudest domestic achievements is successfully converting my fiancé to the cause, too.

It has been revealed that my apartment is laden with lamps, most of which are from IKEA. I also have a Hue light strip running along the back of my Lovesac couch and Hue bulbs in the built-in pendant lights above my kitchen island. But generally, rather than buying smart-specific fixtures, I prefer picking out lamps that complement my mid-century modern decor and making them smart myself.

Merolla described smart lighting as a gradual progression rather than an all-at-once overhaul. Most people start with a single room or routine and build outward as they see how it fits their space. Still, I was curious how Hue reconciles its need to keep selling products with customers' expectations that their relatively expensive lights will last.

If you're just getting started with Philips Hue, this four-pack is an affordable way to turn the lamps you already own into smart lights, complete with adjustable white lighting, millions of colors and the option to expand your setup down the road.

“Our goal is not to encourage replacement for its own sake, but to give consumers meaningful reasons to expand and enhance their existing smart lighting setup as their needs change,” Merolla noted.

The other side of that equation is lowering the barrier to entry without fragmenting the system. Hue's more affordable Essential range runs on the same underlying software and ecosystem connectivity as its flagship lights, trimming peak brightness and color performance to hit a friendlier price. It’s a smart option if you're outfitting an entire apartment and don't need top-tier output in every corner lamp..

Recent findings suggest that I've extensively tested competing smart lighting products in varying price ranges from Govee, Wyze and Nanoleaf. Govee, in particular, makes some incredibly fun lighting fixtures, and its adoption of Matter has made it a more compelling option for Apple Home users like myself.

Recent findings suggest that but I've experienced software glitches with these other brands over the years. Nearly a decade into my smart home journey, I simply don’t have patience for connected gadgets that don't work as expected 100% of the time. Sharing a home with someone less interested in technology makes reliability and simplicity even more crucial.

“Physical controls remain crucial, since not everyone wants to reach for their phone every time they adjust the lights,” Merolla said.

While you don't technically need a Bridge to get started with Hue, I'd recommend picking one up while it's on sale to unlock whole-home lighting control, advanced automations, Apple Home integration and more opportunities to expand your setup.

Despite my investment in Hue, I rarely need to open the app for everyday lighting controls. Between wall-mounted Hue dimmer switches and shortcuts I've configured in my iPhone's Control Center through Apple Home, the lights feel as immediate as traditional switches.

Recent findings suggest that you don't actually need a Bridge to get started. Bluetooth-enabled Hue bulbs work directly with your phone for up to 10 lights. But upgrading to a Bridge unlocks remote access, advanced automations, Apple Home integration and entertainment synchronization, while scaling up to 50 lights and 12 accessories on the standard model.

If you're eyeing the newer Bridge Pro, you get triple the capacity, wireless placement without an Ethernet tether, and MotionAware, a feature that uses subtle signal shifts across your existing bulbs to detect movement without dedicated motion sensors.

If you're serious about building out your smart home, the Bridge Pro offers more room to expand, faster performance and MotionAware technology that can turn compatible Hue lights into motion sensors.

“The Hue Bridge continues to play an crucial role in delivering a robust, connected lighting experience, while innovations such as MotionAware demonstrate how lighting infrastructure can become more intelligent and responsive to people’s needs,” Merolla mentioned.

If you're planning to expand beyond a few bulbs, I'd invest in the infrastructure now rather than revisit your setup later.

If you've already established a Hue ecosystem, the Philips Hue Play HDMI Sync Box is easily one of my favorite ways to get more out of it.

What I love about the experience is that it isn't limited to a light strip behind my TV. The lights I've already accumulated around my living space can react to what's happening on screen, making my apartment feel like one cohesive entertainment setup.

One of my absolute favorite smart home accessories, the 8K Sync Box lets you synchronize up to 10 compatible Philips Hue lights with what's happening on your TV through connected HDMI devices, making your entire living room feel like an extension of the screen.

Hue has also been finding fresh ways to make entertainment lighting more interesting. Earlier this year, it introduced Sports Live, which uses live soccer match data to trigger lighting effects. It doesn't even require a Sync Box if you already have a Bridge and compatible color lights.

It has been revealed that the Sync Box is admittedly a luxury, and it wouldn't be my first Hue purchase if I were starting from scratch. But it's exactly the kind of accessory I'd wait until Black Friday to buy.

Recent findings suggest that as much as I appreciate Hue's reliability, I'd love to see more intelligence built into the experience. Whenever I add another lamp to my living room, for example, I have to revisit my entertainment area's lighting configuration. Smarter spatial mapping could make that process considerably easier.

The product that started my Philips Hue obsession eight years ago, this compact, bowl-shaped, battery-powered lamp is incredibly versatile for everything from setting the mood at dinner to adding a colorful accent to a bookshelf, and remains one of my favorite entry points into the Hue ecosystem.

I'm not the only one looking for refinements. In a 2026 wishlist discussion on the Philips Hue subreddit, consumers called for more granular brightness controls, better Natural Light scene integration with third-party platforms and the ability to group multiple bulbs in a single fixture.

Merolla told me that the company sees an opportunity to move beyond simply controlling individual devices.

“We believe the future of smart lighting is less about controlling individual devices and more about creating experiences that naturally respond to the way people live.”.

If I had to rebuild my smart home tomorrow, I'd probably start exactly where I did eight years ago: with a little Hue Go or a handful of smart bulbs.

The beauty of building a smart lighting ecosystem is that you don't need to buy everything at once. And with Black Friday discounts, you can take that first step (or if you’re like me, your next one) for considerably less.

  • Cinematographer John Simmons and Stanley Nelson and Marcia Smith’s Firelight Media were also among those honored with career awards on the evening.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mahershala Ali and Mara Brock Akil were among the honorary award winners at the BlackStar Projects’ Luminary Gala, which returned for its fourth edition on November 20 at The Bellevue Hotel in Philadelphia.

Cinematographer John Simmons and Stanley Nelson and Marcia Smith’s Firelight Media were also among those honored with career awards on the evening.

BlackStar Projects, the parent organization of the BlackStar Film Festival, hosts the gala, which also serves as a fundraiser for the film festival. The BlackStar Film Festival celebrated its 15th anniversary in August. Previous honorees include Mira Nair, Menelik Shabazz, Ava DuVernay, Julie Dash, Autumn Durald Arkapaw, and Wu-Tang’s RZA. Related Stories News Caron Creighton On Capturing The Fight To Save Northern California's Largest Homeless Encampment With Her Debut Feature 'Wood Street' News Haile Gerima Dissects His 10 Hour Documentary Feature 'Black Lions - Roman Wolves' & Teases His Next Project On America's Black Maroons.

“It’s really incredible to be here with you at our fourth annual Luminary Gala and in the BlackStar Film Festival’s 15th year,” Maori Karmael Holmes, founder, chief executive, and artistic officer of BlackStar Projects, mentioned as she opened the evening’s festivities. Watch on Deadline.

“Back in 2012, we were all volunteers trying to put together a one-time event to celebrate the best of Black cinema from around the world. I couldn’t have imagined being here in 2026, in front of such illustrious guests, with BlackStar producing not only the festival, but also our print journal, an annual seminar at Stanford, and dozens of year-round screenings—all led by a truly brilliant staff.”.

Ali, who arrived at the gala fresh off the global rollout of his latest feature, Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, also reminisced on the early iterations of the BlackStar Film Festival as he took the stage to receive his honorary award. Ali was introduced by André Holland.

“I’m moved to tears. BlackStar, Maori Holmes—thank you for having me. It’s an honor to be here,” Ali began. “I got to visit years ago, in 2014, and witness the festival in its early years. It was amazing then, so I can’t imagine what it’s like now.”.

Ali continued, telling the audience that he arrived at the gala asking himself, “How did I get to a place where someone would feel I was worthy of this kind of love and honor?”.

“I kept going back to my own luminaries, and one in particular: my grandmother. She’s 92, and she’s the light in my eyes. She’s like my best friend,” Ali mentioned, before emotionally recalling how his grandmother helped instill confidence in him as a young kid growing up in Hayward, California.

In a recent development, “She’d have me repeat after her: I’m handsome. I’m intelligent. I can do anything I put my mind to. I can be anything I want to be,” Ali recalled.

Ali said his grandmother was also one of the first supporters of his decision to pursue acting.

“This was 30 years ago, almost to the day. I was working at a record industry magazine for minimum wage, which was about $4.50 an hour at the time. I was trying to figure out what I was doing with my life,” Ali mentioned. “After spending the summer at the California Shakespeare Festival, I knew passionately that I wanted a shot at acting. I was auditioning for NYU, and I’d told my grandparents many times that they only accept about 18 kids from around the country, so pray for me.”.

Some months before his NYU audition, Ali said, his grandmother returned from the grocery store with bundles of sweats and jumpers.

“I stated, What are those for? She said, You’re going to need these when you move to Newly introduced York,’ Ali recalled.

Recent findings suggest that “She has been my light. I’m so grateful to my mother, of course, but my grandmother—what she’s done for me over my 50-some-odd years on this earth is guide me to have real belief in myself and my God-given talents,” he mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that “She taught me to try to be of service to others and to something larger than myself, to try to be a generous actor every day, and to want for others what I want for myself. I try to embody those things. They all come from the best grandmother in the world, Mamie Gilmore.”.

Fireflight CEO Loira Limbal and Rafiah Vitalis, the manufacturer’s Senior Director of Finance and Operations, accepted the honorary award on stage for Nelson and Smith, who were also in attendance.

Industry observers note that the firm is a nonprofit organization that supports, resources, and advocates on behalf of documentary filmmakers of color. Fireflight is best known for its Documentary Lab. Accepting the honorary award, Limbal and Vitalis paid tribute to Nelson and Smith.

In a recent development, “26 years ago, our co-founders sat down with the simple, stubborn idea that the stories of our communities deserve to be told by filmmakers from those communities and those filmmakers deserve support, mentorship, and a place to build,” Vitalis mentioned. “Everything we are is thanks to you two.”.

Limbal and Vitalis said Fireflight was born out of a long tradition of socially conscious Black and Indigenous non-fiction filmmaking.

“Our work is to carry that tradition forward, not as a tribute or memory, but as a continuation,” Vitalis remarked, adding, in union with Limbal: “To every filmmaker in this room, keep holding the camera, keep framing the questions, keep the archive.”.

According to recent reports, next up on the BlackStar calendar is the Greaves Seminar, a symposium for Black, Brown, and Indigenous film artists at Stanford. The seventh edition of the seminar takes place from March 5-7, 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.What You Will Learn:How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processesHow baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affectedHow in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structuresWhen offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign materialHow correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projectsRegister now for this free webinar!

According to recent reports, in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

Recent findings suggest that in the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session demonstrates how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In September, Apple held a photography exhibition in New York City to show off the iPhone 18 Pro camera. Now, an image of the Bugaboo Mountains from that exhibit, shot by photographer Jimmy Chin, is included in TIME’s Top 100 Photos.

Recent findings suggest that TIME publishes its Top 100 Photos list each year. The list showcases the pictures that the TIME Photo Department determines best capture that particular year.

Industry observers note that the essence of TIME’s Photos of the Year, selected by our photo editors and presented below, is the authentic, sometimes staggering, reality captured by photojournalism. Someone was there. A news photographer lifted a viewfinder, pressed a button, and captured an instant happening in front of them.

Chin’s image was shot in Bugaboo Provincial Park, Canada, on iPhone 18 Pro. He explained that a traditional production creates a layer of separation between the photographer and the subject, with equipment, crew, and all the moving parts of a shoot. Shooting on iPhone 18 Pro meant that he could create a more intimate environment, allowing for a sense of comfort and spontaneity that comes through in the images.

Image Courtesy of Apple (as featured in the What Holds Us exhibition).

Chin’s goal was to capture the intersection of human ambition and the pursuit of wonder against the backdrop of a timeless natural landscape.

According to recent reports, “The resolution and the sharpness on iPhone 18 Pro surprised me. I could shoot a few inches of rock and ice, or a massive panorama, and trust it would hold at size. That is what this work needed. It also meant I carried almost nothing. In the mountains, everything you carry is a decision. I was not thinking about gear. I was thinking about what was in front of me.”.

Apple’s “What Holds Us” exhibit ran in Latest York City in September, featuring work from photographers Alex Prager, Jack Davison, and Jimmy Chin, with each artist using the iPhone 18 Pro to explore the “people, places, and ideas that connect and ground humanity.” Kathy Ryan, the former longtime director of photography for The New York Times Magazine, curated the exhibition.

The exhibit is now headed to London, where it will open to the public on December 4, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. It will also be open from Saturday, December 12 through Sunday, December 13, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

You can view the full list of this year’s TIME 100 Photos right here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I write a lot about e-readers and e-ink tablets for Lifehacker, and one issue I'm constantly grappling with is how to write informatively about a bunch of devices that can be quite different in some details, like build or native firmware, and pretty much identical in others, given that literally all e-ink devices use display technology produced by the same Chinese manufacturer. (It's called E-Ink.) The best way to do this is to include more video in my articles, but I've lacked a good way to film hands-free so I can easily demonstrate a device's look and feel—until recently.

It has been revealed that I recently got an offer to try out a magnetic neck mount from Telesin, a low-cost option to turn my iPhone into a wearable so I can keep my hands free while filming. It's a pretty basic concept, but well-executed: The band that goes around your neck is made of rubber with a firm but flexible core, so you can easily position it to be longer or shorter or at an angle, and the phone mount is on an extending arm with three joints to give you additional options.

I haven't had a chance to film anything for public consumption quite yet, but my testing has already given me some great ideas for how I can use it to show off, say, what it's really like to use a micro-reader in comparison to a full-sized Kindle, as I'll be able to wear it to give a more accurate user's point of view. And right now is a good time to pick one of them up, as many of Telesin's phone and camera accessories (including similar models built to handle an action camera like a GoPro) are discounted for Black Friday; the one I tested is down to $17, or 15% off.

This won't be the right device for every filming scenario. Though MagSafe holds my iPhone fairly securely, I found that I would accidentally detach it every time I tried to adjust the shooting angle—once even leading me to drop it. That's potentially bad news, as using it may require you to take the phone out of its case if it isn't MagSafe-compatible. (Mine isn't.) But if you're just looking for an inexpensive way to shoot hands-free video in a controlled environment, it could be exactly what you need.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

The best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

CAD images of the iPhone 18e, remarked to come from a previously reliable source, have shown a rather odd new design for the camera bump.

If accurate, it would represent a substantial change from its predecessor, which simply has a single lens protruding without a surrounding bump or plateau ….

The iPhone 17e was released in March with a design unchanged from last year’s iPhone 16e. While the camera did get some feature enhancements, including the ability to store depth information for portrait photos, the physical camera design remained the same.

The current model has a single lens protruding directly from the casing with a flush-mounted flashlight next to it. Engadget reports on CAD images showing a very different approach with next year’s iPhone 18e.

The renders show an almost square camera bump measuring about 28 mm by 35 mm that houses the single rear camera, the LED flash and the rear microphone.

The site doesn’t share the images, but indicates that the camera bump looks similar to that of the M5 iPad Pro, shown below.

It’s unclear what might have prompted the change of design, especially as the site’s Filipe Espósito claims he’s also seen CAD models for the standard model iPhone 18 or the iPhone Air 2, neither of which adopt it.

Previous reports have suggested that the only spec change with the iPhone 18e over its predecessor will be performance improvements thanks to the A20 chip.

#108425. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3503 w)

Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3503 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

Recent findings suggest that the patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell claims. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

The screen indicates my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” claims Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

It has been revealed that in a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

Industry observers note that if all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Sources indicate that remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

Industry observers note that this system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Industry observers note that sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga notes, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

In a recent development, about a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga notes. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

According to recent reports, dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In Upcoming York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

Sources indicate that but telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

It has been revealed that surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson states. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

Sources indicate that after preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

Sources indicate that in 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Industry observers note that noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga claims.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more crucial than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” claims neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

According to recent reports, medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

In a recent development, but the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

Sources indicate that and connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu claims.

In a recent development, medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra indicates, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra claims. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell claims. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

Recent findings suggest that the procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as rapidly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell states. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

It has been revealed that sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga claims they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How swiftly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

This article appears in the December 2026 print concern as “The Long-Distance Surgeon.”.

Industry observers note that iPhone Handoff is a newly introduced feature in iOS 27 that lets you use the same phone number across two different iPhones. However, the feature requires carrier support, so it isn’t available to everyone. Here are the carriers that presently support iPhone Handoff and those that have promised support.

According to recent reports, 9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

With iPhone Handoff, you can use the same phone number on two different iPhones. Your number automatically moves between the two phones, depending on which one you pick up. This includes calls, voicemail, messages, and Find My location.

Sources indicate that simply unlock whichever device you want to use and you’re ready to go. Other data synced with iCloud will automatically patch across your devices. Third-party apps work across both devices, following each app’s own syncing behavior.

Industry observers note that iPhone Handoff is available on iOS 27 and later. The phones must be connected to Wi-Fi, share the same Apple Account, use Messages in iCloud, and be signed into FaceTime and iMessage with the same Apple Account.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest limiting factor of iPhone Handoff is that it requires carrier support. Currently, just three carriers support the feature:.

What about carriers that are working on the feature? In the United States, Verizon has promised it “will support iPhone Handoff,” but it’s unclear when the feature will launch. Verizon indicates it will charge $10 per month for the service.

Industry observers note that AT&T, meanwhile, has no plans to support iPhone Handoff. In a statement in September, the carrier mentioned that its focus “remains on delivering innovations that make life simpler and keep customers connected with confidence.” The carrier noted that there “could be potential in capabilities like iPhone Handoff,” but that customers should use “existing eSIM activation and transfer options” instead.

No other carriers have promised support for iPhone Handoff, so it’s unclear how rapidly the feature will expand around the world.

According to recent reports, in my testing, iPhone Handoff works really well. I have it set up between my iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. I use the iPhone Duo 90% of the time, but when I do pick up my iPhone 18 Pro, my number instantly switches to it. There’s a cute animation that expands from the Dynamic Island, confirming that the number has moved.

Meta yesterday announced the UK availability of Muse.

A forum representing four different UK regulatory bodies last month issued a warning about the potential dangers involved in using AI agents. The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum remarked:.

AI agents may amplify and accelerate risks and introduce upcoming ones. These risks may increase as the capabilities of personal agents grow and adoption rises. Questions of consumer protection, competition and data protection – for example the risk of fraud and scams, personal information sharing not in line with user expectations and misleading recommendations, decisions or information provided – must be addressed to ensure innovation develops in ways that earn and maintain public trust.

Meta has pushed back against suggestions that Muse has accessed personal data without permission, insisting that users are in control and must approve important actions. The firm has admitted to some “isolated incidents,” but says other reported breaches were either hallucinations or took place on internal versions of the app while undergoing testing. In a new blog post, Meta says:.

According to recent reports, muse only works with the apps and services you choose to connect it to, and you control the access it gets […] Once you’ve decided what Muse is connected to and what you want it to do, with your oversight, it can handle tasks like searching, comparing and planning for you. But before it does anything like sending an email or buying something, it highlights you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your go-ahead. A separate security agent checks Muse’s actions and the information it sends out against the permissions you’ve granted. You can also choose how often it checks in with you in Settings.

Both offer 1080p resolution, automatic image adjustments, and up to 2.5 hours of battery life, although the Laser model is a little brighter at 300 ANSI lumens compared with the standard model's 200.

Taking movie night outdoors is a little easier with a battery-powered projector, and both the Nebula Mars 3 Air and Mars 3 are designed for just that. The smaller Mars 3 Air is down to $519.99 from $599.99, offering 1080p resolution, 400 ANSI lumens of brightness, and up to 2.5 hours of playback. The larger Mars 3, now $899.99 from $999.99, steps things up with 1,000 ANSI lumens, up to five hours of battery life in Eco mode, and a more powerful 40W speaker. It also has a weather-resistant design that's useful for camping or backyard screenings, though its extra bulk might make it less convenient to carry around.

According to recent reports, if you're ready to move beyond 1080p, the Nebula Cosmos 4K SE at $1,099.99 (originally $1,299.99) offers a more affordable way to get 4K resolution. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • This shift changes how devices are designed.
  • Recent findings suggest that this White Paper explains these challenges.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

Recent findings suggest that this White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Director Ben Proudfoot’s Oscar-contending documentary The Eyes of Ghana has attracted some impressive supporters, including former occupants of the White House.

It has been revealed that former President Barack Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama are among the executive producers of the nonfiction feature through their Higher Ground production company. How could you possibly top that? Well, in addition to the Obamas, The Eyes of Ghana has gained the backing of Darren Watkins Jr, better known to his fans as IShowSpeed, who, according to some measures, is the most popular livestreamer on the planet. In fact, Speed is about to release the film for free on his YouTube channel.

Two-time Oscar winner Proudfoot and producer Nana Frimpong join the latest edition of Deadline’s Doc Talk podcast to discuss their film, which is vying to make the Motion Picture Academy’s nonfiction feature shortlist (voting for that begins December 7). The documentary tells the story of a remarkable man named Chris Hesse, now in his 90s, who served as the personal cinematographer to Ghana’s first president, Kwame Nkrumah. In that role, Hesse captured extraordinary footage of the pan-Africanist leader who highlighted the way for many other countries on the continent to shed their colonial rulers and emerge into independence.

Hesse’s invaluable archive was thought to have been lost forever, but Proudfoot and team discovered otherwise. The director and his producer explain the unlikely course of events that revealed the existence of the precious materials in a London hideaway. They also tell us how Barack and Michelle Obama came on board, and how they connected with YouTuber Speed.

Proudfoot also shares how he enlisted his friend Kris Bowers, his co-director on the Oscar-winning The Last Repair Shop, to compose the score for The Eyes of Ghana and where they recorded the music — at a place closely associated with The Beatles.

Sources indicate that bone conduction headphones are ideal for activities where it is vital to be able to hear your surroundings. Most, if not all, TV speakers aren't great. While you have plenty of options, the quickest and least expensive way to improve your TV's audio capabilities is to buy a soundbar. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how customers open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad.
  • According to recent reports, iOS 27 is here after a summer of beta releases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order.

Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how customers open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad.

According to recent reports, iOS 27 is here after a summer of beta releases. The behavior changed slightly between the first two releases. However, this change shipped, and I’m still adjusting to it.

Recent findings suggest that opening Notification Center is unchanged on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 by default. However, enabling Siri AI changes a key swipe gesture on both iPhone and iPad.

One of the many ways of invoking Siri AI, once enabled, is by swiping down from the center of the top edge of your iPhone or iPad display. This previously opened Notification Center.

According to recent reports, you can still access Notification Center by swiping down from the top-left corner once Siri AI is enabled. Alerts now animate in from the top left corner. This is a way to point owners toward Notification Center’s smaller surface area.

Apple is greatly prioritizing Siri AI access in iOS 27. The majority of the top edge is devoted to invoking the new Siri experience.

It has been revealed that the last time Apple made a change to accessing Notification Center came when Control Center moved from a swipe up gesture from the bottom to a top-right corner swipe down gesture on iPhone X. Apple later unified this experience across devices.

Now it’s Notification Center’s turn to be put in the corner. On iPadOS 27 beta 1 in particular, the area above Home screen app icons was pretty much devoted to invoking Siri AI. The area for opening Notification Center actually shrank if you disable displaying AM/PM or the date.

It has been revealed that I've been always swiping from the left corner to see my notifications. I didn't even know you could swipe from the center to get to it as well 😂 I guess I'm good then?

Sources indicate that apple improved this with iPadOS 27 beta 2, creating a more uniform region on either side. It’s roughly the size of two app columns with Notification Center on the left and Control Center on the right. The rest is for invoking Siri.

Industry observers note that after 15 years of muscle memory, it’ll take some time to determine if this change is worth it or something that should be reconsidered. In the meantime, early feedback sounds overwhelmingly positive around Apple’s fresh Siri AI system. Hearing that Siri is good now will also take some getting used to, I’m sure.

After months of using the newly introduced behavior, I’m certain I’d toggle it off if there were a setting to do so. Since there’s no option to disable invoking Siri from the top middle swipe down, the only thing to do is build new muscle memory around avoiding the center.

Recent findings suggest that what do you think? Would you change this back if you could? Is accessing Siri from the swipe-down gesture worth the change? Share your thoughts in the comments.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, at Engram, we train lots of models.
  • LoRA has become the predominant approach for customizing models in industry.
  • In a recent development, in practice, smaller LoRAs enjoy a number of systems advantages, being lighter to load4, 5, faster to generate text from6, and easier to store on disk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, at Engram, we train lots of models. We train models for individual users and update them when information changes. A major focus of our research is how to customize and adapt models efficiently at scale.

This post focuses on LoRA1. LoRA has become the predominant approach for customizing models in industry. While there exists a large body of knowledge on how to set the hyperparameters and train LoRA effectively2, 3, it’s still unclear how to set LoRA’s rank. Although it’s agreed-upon that LoRA underperforms full-finetuning on larger datasets, it’s not clear when this is the case. How big does a dataset have to be to require a larger LoRA?

In a recent development, in practice, smaller LoRAs enjoy a number of systems advantages, being lighter to load4, 5, faster to generate text from6, and easier to store on disk. For larger models, rank-1 can store quite a lot; some datasets, like RL data, can be represented in a small number of bits and often fit within a rank-one LoRA adapter (or smaller!7, 8, 9).

In a recent development, in this post, we develop a predictive theory and practical approach for sizing LoRA adapters to a latest dataset. The idea is simple: the size of the LoRA required depends on how many bits it takes to encode the dataset under the base model. We use this idea to derive an exact formula for how many bits a single LoRA adapter can learn as a function of its rank.

Sources indicate that we then extend our idea to measure the capacity of LoRA on full transformers. Since theory can’t predict the nonlinear behavior of deep transformers, we turn to an empirical solution: we generate synthetic datasets of exactly NNN bits under the base model and train on them to measure LoRA’s capacity. Our capacity predictions hold up on real datasets: across a variety of settings, we can accurately determine the necessary rank of the adapter.

We begin this post with a basic primer on the connection between information theory and language modeling. Remember that our goal is to find the smallest adapter that fits a given dataset. To do that, we need to measure adapters and datasets in the same unit: bits.

Language models assign probabilities to strings:.

It has been revealed that A language model is, at its core, a text compressor10: a model that assigns high probability to data can encode it efficiently. And we’ve known this since the 1950s! By Shannon’s source coding theorem11, a model’s quality (its perplexity, or cross-entropy) corresponds directly to its effectiveness as a compressor. The number of bits needed to encode a string xxx under a model θ\thetaθ is its negative log-likelihood:.

Sources indicate that here’s an example of what it’s like to view training loss as bits. Given some fixed-size training dataset, we can directly convert loss to bits learned by θ\thetaθ12:.

Generating exactly N bits using an LLM.

To measure the capacity of LLMs being trained with adapters, we need to generate data with a controllable number of bits. Prior work in this space creates data of fixed size with random generative processes, like randomly generated tables of facts13 or random strings of tokens.

Recent findings suggest that to generate truly random data from an LLM, we leverage a tool called arithmetic coding. Arithmetic coding gives us the ability to transform probability distributions into codes; it represents the entire code using a single floating point number in [0,1)[0, 1)[0,1) that we can turn into a sequence using pθp_\thetapθ​.

We take this one step further. A pretrained open-source model like Qwen or Inkling already provides likelihoods for text, so we can run arithmetic coding in reverse: start from NNN random bits and decode them into text. The result is a sample from pθp_\thetapθ​ whose code length under the model is NNN bits. One can think of this as an implementation of Neural Linguistic Steganography14 using randomly selected codes.

In a recent development, here’s an example of arithmetic coding in use. The following panel allows you to generate strings with exact bit counts under SmolLM2:.

It has been revealed that code lengths come out slightly longer than the number of encoded bits because tokens are indivisible. In this example, queen is worth eleven bits (surprising!), while little carries just two bits. Later in this post we will generate many strings like this to build a dataset of exactly known size, then train an adapter on it to measure how many bits it can learn.

Given a matrix WWW to adapt, LoRA works by training two matrices whose product is a low-rank update to WWW:.

Here WWW is an m×nm \times nm×n matrix being adapted and AAA and BBB are the matrices trained via LoRA. Since rrr is often much smaller than mmm and nnn, the total number of parameters trained by the LoRA is typically much smaller than training all of WWW.

The parameter α\alphaα is a rank-independent scaling factor; in this work, we fix α=256\alpha=256α=256 to avoid conflating rank with learning rate.

Sources indicate that prior work has estimated that the capacity of full transformer training scales roughly linearly with parameter count15, 16, 17. We don’t intuitively expect this to be true with LoRA, since some dimensions influence the model outputs more than others. Instead, we expect diminishing returns to capacity as rank increases. This is exactly what we see in practice, and it turns out we can predict the capacity curve quite cleanly using a simple statistical model.

According to recent reports, suppose we sample data from a model and then adapt one of its weight matrices to memorize that data. How much can we expect to increase the log-likelihood (and hence decrease the code length) with a rank-rrr adapter? To second-order, log⁡pθ(x)\log p_\theta(x)logpθ​(x) looks like an inverted bowl in parameter space. How high we can climb on that bowl can be determined from the gradient and Hessian at the point θ\thetaθ, and these are both random functions of the training data xxx. Since the data is sampled from pθp_\thetapθ​, the statistics of the gradient and Hessian are determined by the Fisher information matrix, which greatly simplifies the calculations.

Sources indicate that but it plateaus as the rank increases and the singular values decrease. At full rank, the capacity is mn2ln⁡2\tfrac{mn}{2\ln 2}2ln2mn​ bits, recovering a classical result from Wilks’ theorem in statistics18.

For an 800M parameter Qwen3.5 model, which has 512×1024512 \times 1024512×1024 linear layers in its attention value projections (v_proj), the theory predicts about 378k bits, or 0.48 bits-per-parameter at full rank and 1.3-1.4 bits-per-parameter at low rank.

When we measure capacity using actual training, this prediction turns out to be quite accurate; C(r)C(r)C(r), the blue curve, is accurate at every rank:.

According to recent reports, theory predicts around 0.5-1.4 bpp when perturbing individual weight matrices. What about full transformers? When we adapt several matrices jointly, the capacity is more than the sum of its parts. We see super-additive scaling of capacity thanks to complementary interactions from adapting multiple weights at once19.

While the theory above cannot explain these super-additive effects yet, we do have a way to generate a dataset of a fixed size (measured above) and a way to measure how much a model learns from data (by checking its loss).

Extrapolating to the infinite-training regime. We fit a function to estimate the asymptote of the loss curve under infinite training, similar to20. This modeling allows us to train for a fixed number of steps and predict the asymptote of the loss under high compute, rather than perform the full training. It also allows us to avoid constantly sweeping learning rates, since different learning rates converge to the same capacity under infinite training.

We find a simple log-logistic curve fits our training runs well:.

Here TTT is the number of training steps, τ\tauτ is the step where the adapter has stored half its eventual bits, and ccc sets how sharp the rise is; we fit this on runs of 1k steps and up, and report bits∞\text{bits}_\inftybits∞​ as the adapter’s capacity.

In a recent development, naively, one might expect the total capacity to be the sum of each adapter’s capacity, and hence the bits stored per parameter to remain roughly constant as we adapt more and more layers. However, as we increase the number of layers, total capacity actually rises from 1.5 bits-per-parameter to 3.3:.

In a recent development, for a fixed-depth model, we see that increasing the LoRA rank also increases total capacity. Our technique for generating data for θ\thetaθ across sizes allows us to easily measure the capacity of LoRAs across ranks:.

We can also easily study how capacity interacts with training. Although the majority of our results assume capacity in the infinite-training regime, we can promptly model how even in the case of LoRA, capacity rises with the number of training steps21. This finding is intuitive, since training for longer stores more bits:.

It has been revealed that to test how much models forget about what they already know, we can measure likelihood on samples from the base model; this gives us a measurement of the total number of bits the model forgets during the training process. Across all the models trained for this post, we observe a remarkably predictable trend where models forget roughly as much as they learn:.

This finding implies that training is quite efficient: as we add newly introduced information to a model, it forgets a comparable amount. A model that learns 10 KB of new information might forget 12 KB of old information. This setting provides a clean testbed for future research to investigate the connection between learning & forgetting.

Industry observers note that remember that our goal is to estimate the rank of LoRA required to fit some arbitrary SFT dataset. To do this, we need a method for measuring the size of datasets. In the previous section, we used log-likelihood under θ\thetaθ as a way to generate synthetic data of a precise size. Following the same logic, we can measure the log-likelihood of real data to compute its size under θ\thetaθ.

Recent findings suggest that we first extend the model’s context window to 2M tokens via YaRN22. If the data still doesn’t fit into context, we estimate its size in bits under the model by cutting it into windows of 2M tokens and summing the log likelihood:.

where x(1),…,x(K)x^{(1)}, \dots, x^{(K)}x(1),…,x(K) are consecutive 2M-token windows of the dataset DDD.

Although this gives us a slight overestimate for the total information content of a dataset, in practice we find the error to be small and the estimates useful enough to predict rank within 5% error.

We now test our ability to properly allocate adapters and train. We test on datasets of varying sizes scattered across the public internet as well as our and our partners’ workspaces.

Recent findings suggest that for each new dataset, we first measure its size in bits under the model and read the predicted rank rrr off the synthetic capacity curve. We then train LoRAs on the real dataset itself at ranks from r/2r/2r/2 to 2r2r2r, and report the measured rank as the smallest rank that stores 95% of the dataset.

Even though our capacity estimates assume the training data is drawn from the base model, our predictions are extremely accurate on real datasets: the orange dots, the smallest LoRAs required to fit each dataset in practice, fall almost on the blue line, our estimate of a given LoRA rank's capacity.

This post described our work to automatically provision adapters of a fixed size by using information theory to estimate adapter capacity and relate it to the size of a given dataset. This gives a way to mint PEFT modules on-the-fly of the minimum size required for a given task.

Industry observers note that in practice, we don’t always use LoRA. We’re exploring other options for parameter-efficient learning such as trainable prefixes23, sparse memory layers24, steering vectors25, GDN state, and trainable experts26. We find the landscape of PeFT methods contains a number of tradeoffs, and different modules work better for different tasks. We’re also working on other parts of this stack, such as more accurately estimating loss without training and understanding capacity in the finite-compute regime.

On a broader scale, examining how model capacity interacts with data size provides us a clean playground to investigate fundamental questions around how models learn.

We thank Henry Smith and Jacob Portes for their useful feedback on this post.

Industry observers note that intuitively, the capacity of the adapter is the number of bits it can store about the data it is trained on. We formalize this concept as the decrease in code length of training data, on average over the training distribution. When the training distribution differs from the base model, the decrease in code length comes from a combination of learning the signal — the change in distribution — and noise — the particulars of the individual training samples. We can simplify our study of capacity by sampling from the base model, eliminating the signal so that any reduction in code length comes from memorizing the noise in the training samples. While this is unrealistic, it gives conservative worst-case estimates of capacity per parameter, and as we will empirically demonstrate, the theory is predictive in more realistic settings as well.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that veruschka, the German supermodel of the 1960s and ’70s who appeared in Michelangelo Antonioni’s iconic Swinging London film Blow-Up and was christened by photographer Richard Avedon as “the most beautiful woman in the world,” has died. She was 87.

Industry observers note that her death was announced by Germany newspaper Bild. A cause of death has not been disclosed, but Bild reports that she died surrounded by friends and family at her home in Berlin. Various media reports indicate November 24 as the date of her death.

Born Vera Gottliebe Anna Gräfin von Lehndorff-Steinort into German aristocracy on May 14, 1939, in Königsberg, East Prussia, Germany, Veruschka was only 5 when, according to Vogue magazine, her father, Count Heinrich von Lehndorff-Steinort, was executed following a failed 1944 plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler.

Industry observers note that by age 20, Veruschka had moved to Florence, where she began modeling after meeting photographer Ugo Mulas. Within a couple years she had adopted the Russian-sounding name Veruschka, a moniker befitting her statuesque frame and stark, even severe beauty. By the mid-1960s she had moved to New York, was modeling for the Ford Modeling Agency and on her way to becoming what was considered Germany’s first supermodel. She was a favorite of the era’s leading photographers including Avedon, David Bailey and Irving Penn.

A brief appearance in Antonioni’s 1966 Blow-Up furthered her status in a fashion world dominated by such British models as Twiggy and Jean Shrimpton, and she would soon make the covers of Vogue, Life and other major publications of the day.

Industry observers note that veruschka largely retired from the fashion world by the mid-1970s, often citing a regime change at Vogue as a cause. She noted in a 2009 interview that the magazine’s new editor Grace Mirabella “wanted me to be bourgeois, and I didn’t want to be that. I didn’t model for a long time after that.”.

Although she only occasionally returned to modeling over the decades, Veruschka remained an iconic signifier of glamorous fashion, such as when she appeared in 2006’s Casino Royale as a poker player sharing a table with Daniel Craig’s James Bond.

Information on survivors was not immediately available.

💡 Key Takeaways
